Archive absence confirmed:
  $ grep -o "trajectory_events_archive\|trajectory_archive[a-z_]*" package/dist/*.mjs
  (no matches)

By contrast, the transcript tables in the same schema file DO have archive
counterparts (session_transcript_archives, session_transcript_cold_archives) — so the
project already treats archive-before-delete as required for session children. The
trajectory table was simply missed.

I can attach raw snapshot DBs (~300 MB each) or a log slice on request. Not attached
```

### Impact and severity

Severity: Medium-high. Silent, permanent data loss — but low volume per day and no
service outage, so I am not calling it critical.

Impact:

1. Historical analysis is not reproducible. Querying the same closed day twice returns
   different totals. Any per-day cost, usage or activity report built on this table
   drifts without warning between reads. Measured: 25 rows and $0.065 vanished from
   2026-10-24 in ~12 hours.

2. It fails silently. No error, no log line, no counter. The record thins and nobody
   is told. A loud failure would have been fixed in a day; this has been accumulating
   unnoticed.

3. It compounds. Roughly 24 rows/day on one lightly-used workstation is ~720 rows a
   month of history that will never be recoverable, because no archive exists — the
   rows are deleted outright, not moved.

4. It is unrecoverable, not merely inconvenient. session_transcript_archives allow
   transcript recovery after a session is deleted. Nothing equivalent exists for
   trajectory events, so once the cascade fires the usage record is gone for good.
   This is what makes it a defect rather than a retention policy.

5. It blocks a legitimate feature. Per-agent cost attribution and workload/load
   balancing both depend on this table. Anyone building them will produce confidently
   wrong numbers, and the error is invisible — they will not know they are wrong.

Not critical because: no data is exposed, no service is unavailable, no security

boundary is crossed, and the loss per day is small. The defect is in the category of
"quiet corruption of the audit trail" rather than "user-facing breakage."

Scale caveat: the ~24 rows/day figure is from one workstation under one workload and
will vary with session churn. It is a rate, not a constant, and should not be quoted
as a fixed number.

### Additional information

Two related observations, both secondary to the main defect:

1. The same class of loss applies to any analysis I have attempted over past days, so
   I cannot offer prior per-day cost figures as corroboration — they are the thing
   being destroyed. The measurement above is the evidence, not any published total.

2. There is a separate open issue, #148789, about the model fallback chain
   misattributing harness-level session failures to the last fallback model. That is a
   DIFFERENT defect and this report is not a duplicate of it. I mention it only because
   both share a shape: a non-model failure being surfaced in a way that points at the
   wrong layer. Nothing in #148789 concerns trajectory_runtime_events.

What I did NOT do:

- I did not modify the schema, add a trigger, or run any migration against the affected
  database. This report is diagnostic only. Hand-adding a trigger to the one database
  treated as ground truth would risk a schema the product does not understand.
- I did not determine which code path deletes session_windows in normal operation. It
  is not required to confirm the defect: the cascade fires regardless of who initiates
  the delete.
- I did not test whether WAL checkpointing or other operational settings change the
  rate. The rate follows delete frequency, not storage configuration.

Suggested minimum fix: emit a count when the cascade removes trajectory rows, so this
stops being invisible even before archive support lands.

Happy to run any specific query or provide snapshots if that would help.

### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

Static inspection shows that an embedded attempt prepares its tool surface and caller-identity membership callback from a captured conversation capability profile, with no generic hot-reload refresh of that profile found in the reviewed flow; the effect on later tool execution has not been reproduced live.

### Steps to reproduce

Source-level trace (not run live):

1. `prepareEmbeddedAttemptToolBase` captures `runtimeCapabilityProfile` once (`src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt-tool-prepare.ts:247–257`). It passes the profile into tool construction (`:396`) and builds the attempt's tools (`:459`; factory at `:404`, allow filter at `:429`).
2. The caller identity's `assertToolAllowed` callback checks membership against that captured profile via `isConversationToolAllowed(capabilityProfile, …)` (`src/agents/agent-tools.caller.ts:82–92`), without re-resolving policy from current config; this callback definition does not establish that every tool invocation calls it.
3. The only in-attempt reconstruction found is `refreshPermissionMode` (`attempt-tool-prepare.ts:483–503`). It is reached through the `sessions.patch` permissions route (`src/gateway/server-methods/sessions-patch-permissions.runtime.ts:30` → `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run-permissions.ts:19` → `attempt.ts:471–475`). Even that path rebuilds with the same captured profile (`:502` reuses `:396`).
4. Hot reload of `agents.entries` runs only `refreshHooksPolicy` and `reloadInternalHooks` (`src/gateway/config-reload-plan.ts:140–143`, `:208–211`). `tools` is a hot prefix with no action, described as "Prospective operation policy; retained turns and resources keep their own lifetime" (`:261–286`). No reload action that refreshes a running attempt's capability profile was found.
5. For a hot-applied addition to `tools.deny` or the agent's deny list, the reviewed preparation/reload flow has no identified refresh of the captured profile; any later `assertToolAllowed` check using that profile evaluates the pre-change membership policy, while other authority checks can still reject the invocation.

A live reproduction would:
- start a turn that calls `exec` several times in one attempt;
- after the first call, hot-apply `tools.deny: ["exec"]` and wait for the write to report applied;
- observe whether the later calls in the same attempt run.

### Expected behavior

The tool-name policy lifetime for running attempts is not documented. User-facing docs list `agents` and `tools` as hot-applied with no restart (`docs/gateway/configuration/hot-reload.md:251`, `:254`) and do not say that an in-flight attempt keeps its earlier tool policy. Precedents in the same codebase treat authority narrowing as taking effect mid-run:

- An operator role assignment change revokes the in-flight run (`src/gateway/operator-run-authority.ts:491–493`).
- Revoking a node command "cancels its active invocations and rejects later input and results" (`docs/gateway/configuration/hot-reload.md:393–397`).
- #103900 tracks the same class for `tools.exec` settings and is open as a P1 bug.

Requested: narrowing the tool allow/deny policy should apply to later tool calls in a running attempt (fail closed), or the intended "prospective" lifetime should be documented as the contract.

### Actual behavior

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

### OpenClaw version

Source inspected: `main` @ `8c3cf938f1c652cccbd7fd066adffce43af28deb`. No build was tested.

### Operating system

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

### Install method

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

### Model

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

### Provider / routing chain

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

### Additional provider/model setup details

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

### Logs

```shell
NOT_ENOUGH_INFO
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

Source citations above, against the stated commit.

### Impact and severity

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

### Additional information

- Scope: this concerns generic tool-name membership (allow/deny). It does not cover the `tools.exec` mode, security and safe-bin settings tracked in #103900.
- Tool-specific current-state checks exist and are not affected by this finding:
  - delegation grants (`src/agents/delegated-tool-policy.ts:57–71`);
  - browser-loopback grant invalidation (`src/agents/agent-tools.execution-policy.ts:28–40`, `:113–125`);
  - session communication policy (`sessions-send-communication.ts:100–155`);
  - node exec dispatch policy (`bash-tools.exec-host-node.ts:599–615`; test `bash-tools.exec-host-node.integration.test.ts:684–695`, read, not run).
- Retries and fallback: not established either way. `run-attempt-dispatch.ts:448` forwards `params.config`.
- Possible directions (not verified): refresh the capability profile, tool surface and Tool Search catalog when the run's policy inputs change, with pending-call handling like `refreshPermissionMode`; or re-resolve membership against current config in `assertToolAllowed`.
- Related: #103900 (in-flight exec ignores hot `tools.exec` revocation). #107216 and PR #126464 concern config-revision visibility, not enforcement.
- No regression range established.

---
Found and documented by two models working together, with 100% agreement on this text: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic, `claude-opus-5-5`) and GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI, `gpt-6.1-sol`, reasoning effort high). Evidence is a static source review only; nothing was run live.

issues.body:
## Summary

In a Microsoft Teams group chat, the agent the channel routes to answers in a session keyed by the bare chat id. When the
same chat gets a channel-qualified `broadcast` entry, that agent's group-thread turn runs in a different session, keyed by
`conversation:<chat id>`. So adding a broadcast group starts the routed agent on an empty session in that chat, and
removing the entry moves it back to the old session, which lacks everything said in between. The broadcast key that
matches is also `msteams:conversation:<chat id>`, not the `"<channel>:<peerId>"` form the broadcast docs show.

## Version

2026.10.10-beta.5 with `@openclaw/msteams` 2026.10.10-beta.5; the cited code is unchanged on `release/2026.10.10`
(134ba9c7) and on main (dce5fd66).

## What happens

1. Group message in chat A, no broadcast entry: the routed agent runs in `agent:main:msteams:group:19:<chat-a>@thread.v2`.
2. Group message in chat B with `broadcast["msteams:conversation:19:<chat-b>@thread.v2"] = { agents: ["main", "finn"] }`:
   the same agent runs in `agent:main:msteams:group:conversation:19:<chat-b>@thread.v2`.

A key written as the docs suggest, `broadcast["msteams:19:<chat-b>@thread.v2"]`, does not match the chat at all.
Long-term memory is not affected; the session history is.

## Why

- The Teams plugin resolves its ordinary route with the bare conversation id as the peer
  (extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler/message-handler.ts:199-207 on main, peer id at :206; in 2026.10.10-beta.5
  `prepareMSTeamsThreadRouting`, extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler/thread-context.ts:44-52).
- The same plugin sets the reply target to `originatingTo: \`conversation:${conversationId}\``
  (message-handler.ts:497 on main; extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler/inbound-dispatch.ts:228 in 2026.10.10-beta.5),
  and its conversation facts carry no `routePeer` (message-handler.ts:480-486 on main; inbound-dispatch.ts:211-217 in
  2026.10.10-beta.5). For a group chat `nativeChannelId` is also unset (it is only set for channel posts,
  message-handler.ts:415-416 on main).
- `ConversationRoutePeerId` comes only from `conversation.routePeer` (src/channels/inbound-event/context.ts:465 on main,
  :504 in 2026.10.10-beta.5; the field is `ConversationFacts.routePeer`, src/channels/turn/types.ts:82). Slack, Discord,
  Telegram and others set it (for example extensions/slack/src/monitor/message-handler/prepare.ts:1242); msteams does not.
- So `resolvePeer` falls back to `OriginatingTo`, strips the channel prefix and `group:`/`channel:`, but not
  `conversation:` (src/auto-reply/group-thread-dispatch.ts:203-214 on main, :204-215 in 2026.10.10-beta.5). That peer
  selects the broadcast entry (`cfg.broadcast?.[\`${channel}:${peerId}\`]`, src/auto-reply/group-thread-config.ts:13 on
  main, :20 in 2026.10.10-beta.5) and keys each participant's session through `buildAgentSessionKey`
  (group-thread-dispatch.ts:273 on main).

The broadcast docs promise each agent its own session key per room (docs/channels/broadcast-groups.md, "Session
isolation"); for the routed agent that key should be the one it already uses in the room.

## Reproduction (stock runtime)

A scratch gateway with `@openclaw/msteams` and the plugin's own Bot Framework QA stand-in (extensions/msteams/src/qa), two
agents, a channel-wide `msteams` binding to `main`, and a `before_dispatch` hook that logs `ctx.sessionKey`. Send a group
message to chat A (no broadcast entry) and to chat B (with the entry above) and compare the logged keys.

## Expected

The routed agent keeps its session when a broadcast group is added to the chat, and the broadcast key is
`msteams:<conversation id>`, like the other channels. Either fix works:

- the Teams plugin sets `conversation.routePeer = { kind, id: conversationId }` (the same id its route uses), or
- `resolvePeer` also strips a `conversation:` prefix.

The first keeps the plugin's own route and the group-thread peer from drifting again.

## Related, smaller

For a Teams channel post the group-thread peer is `nativeChannelId`, `<team Entra group id>/<channel id>`
(message-handler.ts:415-416 on main), which no documented configuration key names: the docs tell operators to key Teams
config by the conversation ids from Teams links (docs/channels/msteams/access-control.md, "Team and Channel IDs"). A
`routePeer` with the conversation id would fix the channel case too.

Happy to open a PR with the plugin change and a test if that helps.

issues.body:
## Summary

When the Control UI is opened at a name under `.localhost` (for example `http://openclaw.localhost:18789`, which major
browsers resolve to this machine), the Portals page shows **Remote portal ingress required** for a direct portal on
`127.0.0.1`, although the browser is on the Gateway host and the portal opens from **Open in new tab**.

## Version

2026.10.10-beta.5; unchanged on `release/2026.10.10` (134ba9c7) and on main (dce5fd66).

## Problem

`isLoopbackHostname` (ui/src/lib/gateway-locality.ts:1-7, identical in 2026.10.10-beta.5, on `release/2026.10.10` and on
main) accepts `localhost`, `::1`, `[::1]` and `127.0.0.0/8`, but no name under `.localhost`. RFC 6761, section 6.3,
reserves `localhost` and every name under it for loopback, and browsers treat such origins as secure contexts. The
runtime's own server-side check already agrees: `isExplicitLoopbackHostname` counts `hostname.endsWith(".localhost")`
(src/infra/net/ssrf.ts:395-402 on main).

The Portals page reads the Gateway at `ws://openclaw.localhost:18789` as remote and a loopback portal as unreachable
from this browser:

- on main, `ensurePortalProbe` in ui/src/pages/portals/portals-state.ts:362-367 sets `status: "ingress-required"`;
- in 2026.10.10-beta.5, `portalNeedsRemoteIngress` (ui/src/pages/portals/portal-url.ts:16-21), called from
  ui/src/pages/portals/portals-controller.ts:314; built as `vp` in dist/control-ui/assets/control-ui-core-P4iKKKP0.js and
  `Se` in dist/control-ui/assets/portals-page-335hxqpm.js.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Run a gateway bound to loopback and open the Control UI at `http://openclaw.localhost:18789/portals`.
2. Ask an agent to open a portal for a dev server on this machine.
3. The page shows "Remote portal ingress required" instead of offering the portal in a new tab.

## Expected

The page offers the portal in a new tab (its `new-tab-required` state), as it does when the Control UI is opened at
`127.0.0.1` or `localhost`.

## Proposed fix

One function; its other readers (ui/src/api/gateway-connect-errors.ts:48 and
ui/src/components/board/board-widget-frame.tsx:53 on main) move toward the same truth:

```ts
export function isLoopbackHostname(hostname: string): boolean {
  const host = hostname.trim().toLowerCase().replace(/\.$/, "");
  return (
    host === "localhost" ||
    host.endsWith(".localhost") ||
    ["::1", "[::1]"].includes(host) ||
    (/^127(?:\.\d{1,3}){3}$/.test(host) && host.split(".").every((octet) => Number(octet) <= 255))
  );
}
```

with cases beside the existing ones: `isLoopbackHostname("openclaw.localhost")` and `isLoopbackHostname("a.b.localhost")`
are true; `isLoopbackHostname("localhost.example.com")` stays false.

## Why it matters

A `.localhost` name is the usual way to give a local Control UI its own origin (a local reverse proxy, a desktop shell, a
second gateway on the same machine). On such an origin every loopback portal is reported as needing remote ingress, and
the page's advice (Tailscale Serve, a wildcard HTTPS proxy) sends the operator to configure infrastructure that is not
needed.

Happy to open a PR with the change and its test if that helps.

### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

CommandQueueEnqueueOptions still declares taskTimeoutMs, taskTimeoutProgressAtMs, taskTimeoutSubscribe, taskTimeoutAbortSignal, and taskTimeoutAbortGraceMs, but the enqueue implementation no longer reads any of them. The per-task timeout was removed together with the old queue entry runner, and the replacement lane controller only enforces its own lane-level deadline, so a caller that sets taskTimeoutMs gets no timeout at all.

### Steps to reproduce

Enqueue a lane task with taskTimeoutMs: 50 whose promise never settles.
Wait for the advertised budget to elapse.
Observe that the task is never rejected with CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError and the lane stays occupied.

### Expected behavior

Either the declared options are honored (the task is rejected with CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError after the budget plus grace), or the options are removed from the public type so callers cannot silently configure a timeout that does nothing.

### Actual behavior

issues.body:
## Summary

A person who drives a managed browser profile through browser control (the Control UI's Browser panel, or a client
that reaches the gateway's browser routes) has no way to manage the passwords that profile has saved: view one behind
Chromium's own re-authentication, delete one, or import or export a file. The only place those passwords can be managed
is Chromium's own password manager, `chrome://password-manager/`, and browser control refuses to open it or to list it as
a tab. We would like an opt-in, per profile, that lets browser control open and show that one named internal page, with
the runtime still owning navigation and tab selection.

## Who needs this

- The operator of a gateway on a headless or remote host, who drives its managed profile only through the Browser panel.
  The profile saves logins as they sign in to sites, but the saved logins cannot be reviewed, removed or imported.
- A product where several people each drive their own managed profile through the same gateway. Each person reaches only
  their own profile, and only through browser control, never through a window on the machine the browser runs on. For
  them there is no other route to their own saved logins.

In both cases the person can sign in (the browser offers to save the password), yet cannot later see, correct or remove
what was saved.

## Problem

Two hard-coded gates keep every browser-internal page out of browser control, and neither has a setting.

1. **Navigation allows only `http:`, `https:` and `about:blank`.** `assertBrowserNavigationAllowed` throws
   `Navigation blocked: unsupported protocol "chrome:"` for any other scheme
   (extensions/browser/src/browser/navigation-guard.ts:15-16 for `NETWORK_NAVIGATION_PROTOCOLS` and
   `SAFE_NON_NETWORK_URLS`, :105-123 for the check, the throw at :121, on main at dce5fd6; :15-16 and :100-115 at
   v2026.10.10-beta.5, bundled as `dist/chrome-DTxOHDcD.mjs:207-208`, `:246-251`). Every open and navigate path calls it:
   - `openTab` (extensions/browser/src/browser/server-context.tab-ops.ts:372, the checks at :383 and :445 on main; :396
     and :448 at beta.5, `dist/server-context-CLdT7m_2.mjs:889`, `:940`);
   - `POST /tabs/open` (extensions/browser/src/browser/routes/tabs.ts:239, the check at :264 on main);
   - `POST /navigate` (extensions/browser/src/browser/routes/agent.snapshot.ts:123, the check at :148 on main; :133 and
     :158 at beta.5).
2. **Tab listing drops every browser-internal target.** `isSelectableCdpBrowserTarget` rejects any URL starting with
   `chrome://` (and `chrome-untrusted://`, `chrome-extension://`, `devtools://`, `edge://`, `brave://`, `vivaldi://`,
   `opera://`) (extensions/browser/src/browser/cdp-target-filter.ts:7-16 and :29-31 on main; :7 and :30 at beta.5,
   `dist/cdp-target-filter-23Uc36pP.mjs`). `readTabs` applies it on both enumeration paths
   (server-context.tab-ops.ts:207 and :241 on main; :233 and :267 at beta.5, `dist/server-context-CLdT7m_2.mjs:784`,
   `:808`), and `openTab` refuses a created target that resolves to one ("Failed to open tab (non-selectable target)",
   :526-528 on main). So even a page the person opened by hand cannot be selected, screenshotted or acted on by target id.

The filter's own comment gives the reason: "Browser-internal pages cannot be reliably automated as user content"
(cdp-target-filter.ts:4-5). That reason is sound for agents, and the filter came from real problems (#55734, an agent
navigating into `chrome://omnibox-popup.top-chrome/`; fixed by #80629, extended by #103115 and #162110, and #184799 adds
`chrome-search://`). But it also removes the one page a person needs to manage their own saved passwords, and the docs
offer no way back: docs/tools/browser-control.md ("Security and privacy", :560-586 on main) and
docs/tools/browser/configuration.md name no setting for internal pages, and docs/tools/browser/profiles.md:62-63 says
"Blank or internal pages remain ordinary tool results".

## Proposal (for the maintainers to shape)

A per-profile opt-in allowlist of named internal pages, off by default:

```json5
{
  browser: {
    profiles: {
      work: {
        // default: [] (today's behaviour)
        allowInternalPages: ["chrome://password-manager/"],
      },
    },
  },
}
```

- For a profile that lists it, `open`, `navigate` and `/tabs/open` accept URLs under that exact prefix, and the tab list
  keeps a target under it, so the person can select it as a tab and the Browser panel can show it (screencast or
  screenshot, click, type). Every other internal URL stays refused and filtered, so #55734 stays fixed.
- Named pages only, not a scheme switch: `chrome://password-manager/` is the case here.
- For the person's own hands, not the agent: the agent `browser` tool keeps refusing these pages (no snapshot, text
  extraction or evaluate), so a model never receives the page's contents. #186692 (autofilled password values in
  snapshots) shows why password material should stay out of tool results.
- Chromium's own re-authentication before a password is revealed, exported or edited stays as it is; the runtime adds
  no bypass and never reads values itself.
- The runtime keeps owning navigation and tab ownership: the opt-in is one more entry in the existing navigation policy
  and target filter, not a separate channel.

Alternatives, if an allowlist is not the shape you want: a `browser passwords` verb (list origins and usernames, remove,
import a CSV) that drives the password manager itself and never prints a password, or a documented hook that lets an
embedding host route the internal page to a viewer it trusts.

## Why it matters

Browser control is the only way to reach a managed profile on a headless or shared host, and the profile already saves
logins. Without this, saved passwords there are write-only: a wrong or stale login cannot be fixed, a leaked one cannot
be removed, and moving to the managed profile means re-typing every login. An embedding product that wants to help could
only do it by driving the browser's DevTools channel itself, outside the runtime's navigation policy and tab ownership,
which is worse for everyone. A narrow, opt-in, person-only allowlist keeps the policy in the runtime.

## Evidence (runtime 2026.10.10-beta.5, and main at dce5fd6)

- extensions/browser/src/browser/navigation-guard.ts on main: the scheme sets at :15-16, `assertBrowserNavigationAllowed`
  at :105-123 (throw at :121). The same gate at v2026.10.10-beta.5 (:15-16, :100-115), on release/2026.10.10 (same blob
  as beta.5) and in v2026.10.9. Main adds only an `assertNavigationCurrent` fence (:55, :113, :158); the scheme check is
  unchanged.
- extensions/browser/src/browser/cdp-target-filter.ts on main: the prefix list at :7-16 with `chrome://` at :8,
  `isSelectableCdpBrowserTarget` at :29-31. Identical at beta.5 apart from one doc comment.
- extensions/browser/src/browser/server-context.tab-ops.ts on main: `readTabs` filters at :207 and :241, `openTab` at
  :372 checks at :383 and :445 and refuses a non-selectable created target at :526-528.
- extensions/browser/src/browser/routes/tabs.ts:264 and routes/agent.snapshot.ts:148 on main: the open and navigate
  routes call the same check.
- docs/tools/browser-control.md on main: no setting for internal pages; the beta.5 to main diff of this page changes
  only formatting and one sentence about `evaluate`.
- Open #167703 (native page navigation) reworks the navigation guard but keeps the same scheme check (`http:`, `https:`,
  `about:blank`). Open #184799 extends the target filter with `chrome-search://`. We found no issue or pull request,
  open or closed, that asks for or adds an internal-page allowlist.
- Related: #55734, #80629, #184799, #186692.

issues.body:
## Summary

`ScreenRecordService.record` clamps before recording (`ScreenRecordService.swift:38-39`: duration to 250–60000 ms, default 10 s; fps to 1–60, default 10), but the runtime echoes the raw request into the payload:

```swift
// apps/macos/Sources/OpenClaw/NodeMode/MacNodeRuntime.swift:683-689
durationMs: params.durationMs,
fps: params.fps,
screenIndex: params.screenIndex,
```

`camera.clip` does this right (`:515`, the service's value). The agent tool surfaces `payload.durationMs`/`payload.fps` in its result (`src/agents/tools/nodes-tool-media.ts:296-297`), so a `screen_record durationMs=120000` returns a 60 s clip labelled 120000 ms, an omitted duration returns a 10 s clip with no `durationMs` at all, and `fps: 120` records at 60 and reports 120.

## Environment

- openclaw `main` @ `fefc2fb01ca`
- macOS 27.0 (Darwin 27.0.0), Xcode 27 toolchain, Apple Silicon
- `apps/macos` Swift Testing (`swift test`) against the real code; nothing mocked except where stated

## Reproduction

Real `MacNodeRuntime.handleInvoke` with an injected `recordScreen` that records what it was asked for:

```
[repro3] L3-26 request durationMs=120000 fps=120 → service clamps to 60000/60.0; payload reports durationMs=Optional(120000) fps=Optional(120.0)
✘ Expectation failed: payload.durationMs == clampedDuration
✘ Expectation failed: payload.fps == clampedFps
[repro3] L3-26 omitted duration → payload durationMs=nil (service default 10000)
✘ Expectation failed: barePayload.durationMs == CaptureRateLimits.clampDurationMs(nil)
```

## Expected

Report the clamped values the service used, the way `camera.clip` does.

issues.body:
### Environment

- OpenClaw `2026.9.5 (ec9c1a1)`, npm global install at `/opt/homebrew/lib/node_modules/openclaw`
- macOS 27.0 (arm64, Mac mini), Node `v24.21.0`
- Channel `openclaw-weixin` with two configured accounts

### Summary

An automation created through the **`automations` tool by the agent** is stamped with an account-scope imprint:

```json
"scheduledToolPolicy": {
  "version": 1,
  "mode": "account",
  "ownerSessionKey": "agent:main:main",
  "ownerAccountId": "af3a63dfd16a-im-bot"
}
```

Every subsequent run aborts **before reaching the model**, in 12–46 ms, with:

```
Scheduled account "af3a63dfd16a-im-bot" is unavailable.
Re-add it to the channel configuration, or recreate this automation from the intended account.
```

The account is in fact configured and fully working at the same moment:

- `openclaw channels list` → `openclaw-weixin` installed / configured / enabled
- `~/.openclaw/openclaw-weixin/accounts.json` → `["af3a63dfd16a-im-bot","88b3d0c659ab-im-bot"]` (mtime unchanged for days)
- another scheduled job using the identical delivery `channel` + `to` + `accountId` delivers successfully
- ad-hoc messages through that same account deliver successfully

So this looks like a **fail-closed false positive**, not a real misconfiguration.

### Steps to reproduce

1. From a chat session, create an automation with the `automations` tool, with delivery
   `{ "mode":"announce", "channel":"openclaw-weixin", "to":"<id>@im.wechat", "accountId":"af3a63dfd16a-im-bot" }`.
2. Trigger it (`automations` → `run` / `runMode:"force"`) or wait for its schedule.
3. The run fails with the message above in ~12–46 ms; the model is never invoked; `automations runs` shows the error.

### Workaround (works reliably)

Recreate the **same** job with the operator CLI:

```bash
openclaw cron add \
  --name "月度安全自检" --display-name "月度安全自检（本机）" \
  --description "..." \
  --cron "0 9 1 * *" --tz "Asia/Shanghai" \
  --session isolated \
  --message "$(cat message.txt)" \
  --timeout-seconds 600 \
  --announce --channel openclaw-weixin --to "<id>@im.wechat" --account "af3a63dfd16a-im-bot"
```

The CLI-created job is stamped `scheduledToolPolicy.mode = "trusted"` and runs immediately and correctly with an **identical payload and delivery**. This shows the payload/delivery are valid and only the guard path differs. Rebuilding in the Control UI / Automations page is also a workaround.

### Where it appears to fail (read from the 2026.9.5 dist bundle; line numbers may shift)

- `dist/agent-tools.policy-*.mjs` — `unavailableScheduledAccount()` (~line 310) produces that error text. It is only reachable when `requireConfiguredAccount === true`.
- `dist/run-executor.runtime-*.mjs` — the cron executor sets `requireConfiguredAccount` when `scheduledToolPolicy.mode === "account"`, resolving
  `messageProvider = sourceDelivery.target.channel ?? resolvedDelivery.channel` and `accountId = ownerAccountId`.
- The gate is roughly `plugin.config.listAccountIds(cfg).some(id => normalizeAccountId(id) === accountId) === true`; otherwise it fails closed.

Any of the following would explain the observed behaviour and would be worth checking:
- `listAccountIds` for `openclaw-weixin` not enumerating accounts in this environment (it works for delivery, so the two paths disagree);
- `messageProvider`/`accountId` resolution producing a provider/account pair that the guard cannot match.

### Expected behaviour

- If the account **is** configured for that channel, the run should proceed — the guard should resolve accounts the same way the delivery path does.
- If it must fail closed, the reason should be diagnosable: at minimum log the resolved `messageProvider`, `accountId`, and the account ids actually seen, so a false positive can be told apart from real misconfiguration. Right now the job silently aborts with no clue.

### Impact

- Every agent-created automation that targets a specific configured account is permanently broken until manually recreated through the CLI / Control UI.
- Because the run aborts before the model is invoked, failures produce no useful output and are easy to miss.

### Extra notes from the same host (possibly related, lower confidence)

- The gateway log shows `memory pressure` warnings on this host around the time of the failures
  (`level=warning rss=1.76–1.96 GiB heap≈670–715 MiB threshold=512 MiB`), with the log recommending
  `openclaw gateway status --deep` / `openclaw gateway diagnostics export`.
- Separately observed once: an `exec` tool call sat in "auto-review" with **no timeout and no log line** for ~15 minutes, until the stuck-session watchdog aborted the embedded run
  (`reason=blocked_tool_call activeWorkKind=tool_call lastProgress=tool:exec:started`, then
  `stuck session recovery … action=abort_embedded_run` → `AbortError: agent run superseded by a newer session writer`).
  Reported only in case the approval layer and the account guard share a code path.

issues.body:
### Summary

Add an optional wrap-up reserve to the fixed per-run budget (`agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds`). At `timeoutSeconds - wrapUpSeconds`, the run gets a signal to stop researching and answer with what it has. Today the run is simply aborted at the hard deadline. Separately, expose the run's deadline to plugins so they don't have to reconstruct it.

### Problem to solve

`timeoutSeconds` is a single elapsed-time budget per run (on the Codex harness, anchored to attempt start). Nothing tells the model that time is running out. A tool-heavy research run, for example on a messaging channel, keeps calling browser and shell tools until the abort. The user gets no answer at all, even when the run had already gathered most of what it needed.

In our installation, every timed-out run in a 30-day window was this shape:
- 41–56 tool calls each;
- no hung or slow tool (the longest single call was about 10 s);
- the last tool result arrived within about 20 s of the cutoff;
- no answer was delivered.

Successful runs of the same kind finished well inside the budget. Once a run stops calling tools, writing the final answer took p90 about 30 s and at most about 95 s.

### Proposed solution

1. **Config:** `agents.defaults.wrapUpSeconds` (default off), also allowed per agent.
2. **Behavior at `startedAt + timeoutSeconds - wrapUpSeconds`:**
   - inject a system/developer note telling the model to stop and answer now, listing what is still unverified;
   - optionally refuse further non-messaging tool calls, with a clear reason returned to the model.
   - The clock is never reset by a fallback attempt within the same run.
3. **Plugin API:** expose `deadlineAt`, or `startedAt` plus `timeoutMs`, on the tool-policy / `before_tool_call` context.
   - Plugins could then implement their own policy without reading config or correlating lifecycle events across instances.
   - Today the trusted tool policy and lifecycle subscribers can run on separate plugin instances, so a plugin has to coordinate the run start through files.
4. **Terminal outcome:** a run that finished after a wrap-up reports a distinct status (e.g. `partial`). Downstream tooling can then tell it apart from a normal completion and from a timeout.

### Alternatives considered

- **Raising `timeoutSeconds`.** This moves the cliff without removing it, and long runs stay silent until the abort.
- **Progress-idle / renewable timeouts (#144327, #77626).** These solve a different problem, keeping active work alive. They don't give the model a chance to answer before a hard stop. The two approaches can coexist.
- **A plugin.** We run one: a trusted tool policy that blocks research tools in the reserve window, plus a lifecycle subscriber. It works, but it has to infer the deadline from config and the run start from lifecycle events written to disk. It also cannot nudge a model that is thinking rather than calling tools.

### Impact

Runs on messaging channels with fixed budgets would end with a partial answer instead of nothing. This applies to any tool-heavy agent near its budget (research, browsing).

### Evidence/examples

See Problem: all three timed-out runs show the same pattern, many short tool calls right up to the abort. We now enforce a 150 s reserve with the plugin described under Alternatives.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

No, not at this time.

### Additional information

Happy to share the plugin's approach (tool-policy block reason text, reserve sizing) if it helps.

issues.body:
Replying to a bot-sent Telegram photo makes that photo available to the agent as reply context. The original report treated that hydration as a bug and proposed dropping every bot-authored reply attachment. That conclusion was too strong: current source and existing tests intentionally preserve inspectable reply photos, and loss of bot attribution before the provider request has not been demonstrated.

## Current evidence

Checked against `main` `2e7668b2eaad12171ef4421b68286de6063b7e77` on October 24, 2026:

- `extensions/telegram/src/bot-message-context.session.ts` puts current attachments in `media` and reply attachments in `supplemental.quote.media`, alongside the reply sender and body. Hydration alone does not prove the bot photo is presented as a new user attachment.
- `extensions/telegram/src/bot.test.ts` explicitly covers `hydrates allowlisted group reply ancestors`, including a bot-authored photo and the sender label `OpenClaw (you)`.
- This source inspection is not a live Telegram-to-provider capture. The reported model confusion and any later loss of attribution remain unproven.

## Reproduction to distinguish the claims

1. Have the bot send a photo in an isolated Telegram test conversation.
2. Reply to that photo with a question about it and no new attachment.
3. Capture the incoming reply identity, the Gateway's current-versus-quoted media projection, and the final provider request for the same turn.
4. Check whether the image remains attributed to the bot's earlier message and whether the answer addresses the reply.

A reply carrying a distinct new photo is the control: the current image and quoted bot image should remain distinguishable. Source inspection and an image-loader unit test do not establish this final request behavior.

## Product decision

The proposed unconditional self-authored guard would prevent users from asking about photos the bot previously sent. Preserve the existing inspection behavior unless a Telegram owner chooses otherwise. If a captured turn loses attribution, repair the boundary that loses it instead of assuming all bot-photo hydration should be removed.

PR #155273 addresses a separate case: the same Telegram source present in both current and replied-to media. It deliberately preserves bot-photo inspection and does not close this issue. Earlier exclusion proposals #57280 and #66912 closed unmerged.

The original root-cause and fix sections are withdrawn. This issue stays open for the attribution capture and the owner's reply-photo contract decision; no new exclusion fix is requested.

issues.body:
## Summary

The built-in `computer` tool always returns `COMPUTER_DRIVER_UNAVAILABLE: the Gateway desktop provider is unavailable` when a non-main agent calls it with the default route (Gateway desktop). Main-agent calls work, but only because they resolve to a paired node instead.

## Root cause (code-level)

`dist/gateway/desktop/computer.worker.js`, in the `start` handler:

```js
await ensureNodeHostPluginRegistry({
    ...context,
    onlyPluginIds: pluginIds,
    commandAllowlist: new Set(["screen.snapshot", "computer.act"]),
    ...
});
const declaration = listRegisteredNodeHostCapsAndCommands(context);
if (!declaration.computerUse || !declaration.commands.includes("screen.snapshot"))
    throw new Error("COMPUTER_DRIVER_UNAVAILABLE: the Gateway desktop provider is unavailable");
```

The worker always passes a non-empty `commandAllowlist`. Inside `listRegisteredNodeHostCapsAndCommands` (`bin/node-host/plugin-node-host.ts`):

```ts
if (!options.commandAllowlist && entry.command.computerUse)
    computerUse = parseComputerUseCapabilityDescriptor(entry.command.computerUse(context));
```

Because the allowlist is always present for the Gateway worker, `computerUse` can never be populated. The subsequent guard therefore always throws, so the Gateway desktop path can never become available regardless of configuration.

## Impact

- Every agent on this gateway that omits `target` (or passes `target: "gateway"`) fails on the first `computer` action with a misleading "provider is unavailable" message.
- Enabling the Peekaboo Bridge toggle in **Settings → This Mac → Capabilities**, granting Accessibility and Screen Recording, and switching providers between Peekaboo and CUA make no difference — the failure happens before any driver is consulted.
- The diagnostic message suggests a permissions or provider problem, so users spend time re-checking settings that cannot affect the outcome.

## Reproduction

1. Have a secondary agent (not the gateway's primary session) call the computer tool:
   ```json
   {"action": "screenshot", "target": "gateway"}
   ```
2. Observe: `{"status":"error","error":"COMPUTER_DRIVER_UNAVAILABLE: the Gateway desktop provider is unavailable"}`
3. Same call with `target: "node"` succeeds immediately on the same host, with the same permissions.

## Expected

Either:
- `computerUse` is populated for the Gateway worker despite the command allowlist (the allowlist exists to restrict dispatchable commands, not to disable capability advertisement), or
- the guard distinguishes "no provider registered" from "capability suppressed by allowlist", and the error message says which one applies.

## Environment

- macOS 26.5.1 (arm64), OpenClaw app 2026.10.6
- Gateway local, `desktop.host.enabled: true`, tool profile `full`
- Accessibility + Screen Recording granted; Peekaboo Bridge toggle on
- Six agents configured; only the primary one can reach `computer`

issues.body:
### Summary Let `openclaw backup restore --target ` import the archive's PostgreSQL stores through an operator-supplied connection (for example `--postgres-connection ` or a per-restore override file) instead of only the connection recorded in the archived `openclaw.json`. ### Problem to solve For an archive that contains PostgreSQL stores, restore validates the captured configuration and imports every store into a fresh `restore_` namespace over the connection that captured config resolves to. This matches the docs (gateway/postgresql.md "Restore all PostgreSQL stores", cli/backup.md). The docs' answer for recovering elsewhere is to "point that secret at the recovery server". That only works when the connection is an env SecretRef. Our production connection is a file SecretRef with an absolute path (`secrets.providers.

= {source:"file", path:"~/.openclaw/secrets/postgres-dsn"}`). On the same host the archived config resolves that path to the production DSN file. The only ways to redirect it are rewriting the production secret file, which the running Gateway reads, or unpacking, editing and repacking the archive, which defeats verify-then-restore. An exec SecretRef has the same problem. So we can't rehearse a restore, or verify a backup by restoring it, without writing new schemas into the production database. Our planned restore drill of the production archive is blocked on this. `backup restore` has no option for it: its CLI options are `--from`, `--namespace` (a remote storage namespace, not a database namespace), `--target` and `--json`. `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`, `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` and libpq env vars don't change the import connection (see Evidence). ### Proposed solution Add an explicit restore-time connection override for PostgreSQL imports, for example: ``` openclaw backup restore --target

\ --postgres-connection file: # or env:VAR / a SecretRef JSON ``` Desired behavior: - All PostgreSQL imports, and the discard of new namespaces after a failed restore, use the override connection. The captured family selections are unchanged. - The restored `openclaw.json` either keeps the captured connection (it is a staging rehearsal) or records the override, chosen by an explicit flag. Either way the output states which connection the anchors point to, so activation doesn't silently attach to the wrong server. - Optionally `--schema-prefix

` so restored namespaces are `

_…`, not `restore_`, on a shared server (related: #181858, where `database port` ignores `schemaPrefix`). - `backup verify` keeps working without a database. The override is only needed for restore. ### Alternatives considered - **Point the secret elsewhere (documented):** works for env SecretRefs. We tested this; it is Attempt C in Evidence. It doesn't work for file or exec SecretRefs on the production host without touching the live secret. - **Restore on a different host** where the same absolute secret path holds a staging DSN: possible, but it needs a second machine laid out with the production paths just for a drill. - **Unpack, edit the captured config, repack:** not tried. It changes the archive under test, so it no longer proves that the production archive restores. It may also fail archive verification. - **Restore into production and drop the `restore_*` schemas afterwards:** this is what happens today. It writes full copies of every store into the production database and risks dropping the wrong schema. - **Switch production to an env SecretRef:** changes the production secret setup only to work around a missing restore option. ### Impact - Affected: self-hosted operators whose PostgreSQL connection uses a file or exec SecretRef. That is the setup the PostgreSQL docs show for socket DSNs. - Severity: blocks the workflow. There is no non-production way to run a restore drill or verify-by-restore on the production host. - Frequency: every restore drill or backup verification by restore. - Consequence: each full restore writes a complete copy of every store into the production database (98 tables per state namespace in our test). Or the drill doesn't happen, and the backups are never restore-tested. ### Evidence/examples Reproduced on a scratch install pointed at an isolated test database (`openclaw_ci`), with the `state` family ported to PostgreSQL (schemaPrefix `issue3`). Workboard had no store in the minimal scratch, so `database port --family workboard` was a "verified no-op". The state store shows the same behavior. Redacted: DSNs; `/Users/openclaw` replaced with `~`. Help text, no connection or database option: ``` $ openclaw backup restore --help Usage: openclaw backup restore [options] Options: --from Read a backup key or latest from a storage location -h, --help Display help for command --json Output JSON (default: false) --namespace Backup namespace (default: sanitized hostname) --target

Fresh target directory; non-empty directories are refused ``` Setup and archive: ``` $ openclaw database port --family state --to postgres Database port: complete (postgres); 1 database stores. $ openclaw backup create --output ~/issue3/archives --verify Backup archive: ~/issue3/archives/2026-10-24T11-14-15.462-07-00-openclaw-backup.tar.gz Archive verification: passed ``` The manifest lists `postgresSnapshots: [{"archivePath": ".../state/state/openclaw.sqlite.postgres", ...}]`. Baseline restore. BEFORE: ``` openclaw_ci|issue3_state_58ae7737f87148c5 ``` ``` $ openclaw backup restore ~/issue3/archives/2026-10-24T11-14-15.462-07-00-openclaw-backup.tar.gz --target ~/issue3/restored Backup archive restored to staging: ~/issue3/restored Archive entries restored: 28 ``` AFTER (database, schema, table count). A new namespace appears in the same database: ``` openclaw_ci|issue3_state_58ae7737f87148c5|98 openclaw_ci|restore_d7e1f14ef55149d9b6f8f0e8652d2867|98 ``` The restored anchor (`state/openclaw.sqlite`, table `openclaw_engine_anchor`) points there: ``` ('58ae7737-f871-48c5-be5f-52e1f6244799', 'postgres', 'restore_d7e1f14ef55149d9b6f8f0e8652d2867') ``` The restored `openclaw.json` still carries the original connection: ``` "secrets": {"providers": {"pgci": {"source": "file", "path": "~/pgtest-dsn", "mode": "singleValue"}}}, "database": {"postgres": {"connection": {"source": "file", "provider": "pgci", "id": "value"}, "schemaPrefix": "issue3"}, "families": {"state": {"engine": "postgres"}}} ``` Attempts to redirect the import to a staging database. For these I made a second DSN file, identical except that dbname is `openclaw_ci_staging`. That database doesn't exist, so a redirected import should fail to connect. - **A. Different live config:** `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR=~/issue3/alt OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH=~/issue3/alt/openclaw.json`, where that config's `pgci` provider points at the staging DSN file. Restore succeeded and created `restore_d1959f939188438f94be81bdbe94f5b7` in `openclaw_ci`. The live config is ignored, which matches "The live installation's selections do not override the archive". - **B. libpq env:** `PGDATABASE=openclaw_ci_staging`. Restore succeeded and created `restore_d1a75c1948524b46a2282dfa40c5ea81` in `openclaw_ci`. The DSN's dbname wins. - **C. Env SecretRef (the documented lever):** a second scratch archive whose connection is `{source:"env", provider:"default", id:"OPENCLAW_DATABASE_DSN"}`, restored with that variable set to the staging DSN. This one is redirected: - From a SQLite-only state dir, restore tried the staging database: `PostgreSQL restore failed ...: no pg_hba.conf entry for host "[local]", user "...", database "openclaw_ci_staging"`, and it created nothing in `openclaw_ci`. - Run with `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` set to that PostgreSQL-backed scratch, the same variable also redirected the restoring install's own state-ownership check: `Cannot admit backup.create ... failed to acquire gateway state ownership | Cannot open PostgreSQL connection ... database "openclaw_ci_staging"`. So even this route ties one variable to both the restoring host's live state and the restore target. - **File SecretRef:** I found no override short of editing the referenced secret file, which here is the production DSN file, or modifying the archive. I didn't try modifying the archive. Source (main 794d6500f38): - `src/cli/program/register.backup.ts:71-89`: restore options are only `--from`, `--namespace`, `--target` and `--json`. - `src/commands/backup-restore.ts:277-279`: `backupRestoreCommand(runtime, options: { archive: string; target?: string; json?: boolean })`. - `src/commands/backup-restore.ts:141-260` (`restorePostgresExports`): `runOfflineDatabaseBackup` is called with `configPath: path.join(targetPath, recoveryConfigContextPath ?? recoveryConfigPath)` and `configSourcePath: configPath` (lines 247-252), so the config is always the archived one, with `env: { ...process.env, ... }`. Then `preparePostgresRestore({ ..., config, ... })` runs at lines 195-202. - `src/snapshot/database-backup.ts:76-97`: reads that captured config and calls `resolveDatabaseEngineSelection(config)`. - `src/snapshot/database-backup.operations.ts:143`: `withDatabasePortConnection(params.config, ...)`, the connection the import uses. - `src/infra/database-engine/port-provider.ts:51-65`: resolves the postgres input from that config and env. No override parameter. - `src/snapshot/database-backup-core.worker.ts:172`: ``const namespace = `restore_${randomUUID().replaceAll("-", "")}` ``, which ignores `schemaPrefix`. Our build 98f1a668 vs main 794d6500f38: `git log 98f1a668..origin/main` on these files shows only `012d92f5378` (#182405), which moved the restore worker code from `database-backup.ts` into `database-backup.operations.ts`, plus docs edits unrelated to restore. The connection resolution is unchanged, so this should behave the same on main. I didn't run it on main. ### Do you plan to open a PR for this? No, proposing the idea only ### Additional information - Version: OpenClaw 2026.10.6 (main 98f1a668), source checked against main 794d6500f38. OS: macOS (Darwin 27). Install: git checkout of main. PostgreSQL 17 over a Unix socket. - Duplicate search (`gh search issues --repo openclaw/openclaw --include-prs`): "backup restore postgres", "postgres restore", "PostgreSQL backup", "postgresql archive restore", "restore staging database", "backup restore connection", "restore different database", "backup restore target database", "restore recovery server", "restore SecretRef", "restore drill", "restore namespace schemaPrefix". Nothing matched. Related but different: #178971 (local Gateway checkpoints that don't touch PostgreSQL), #181858 (`database port` ignores `schemaPrefix`; restore's `restore_` naming is the same pattern), #155599 (general backup features). - Suggested fix direction: thread an optional connection override from the `backup restore` CLI through `backupRestoreCommand` and `restorePostgresExports` into `runOfflineDatabaseBackup`. Apply it to the resolved postgres input when building the engine selection: it replaces only `database.postgres.connection` and keeps the captured family selections. Use the same override for `discardPostgresRestores`. Resolve it separately from the restoring host's own state-ownership checks, so a staging connection can't be confused with the host's live database. Report the target connection identity (host/db/user, redacted) in the restore result, and make the restored config's connection explicit (keep the captured one, or write the override) so activation doesn't attach anchors to the wrong server. An optional restore-time `schemaPrefix` would make rehearsal namespaces on a shared server easy to find and remove.

issues.body:
## Summary

The gateway process (`dist/index.js gateway`) leaks memory at ~23 MB/min under normal load. On a macOS arm64 host it climbed from ~2.3 GiB after boot to **4.07 GiB RSS** in ~1h33m, triggering two **CRITICAL memory-pressure events** (`reason=rss_growth`, `rssGrowth` up to 1.22 GiB). The leak is in the `session-transcript.worker.js` worker pool: workers are never retired, and each one pins a hydrated transcript in memory.

## Environment

- **OpenClaw 2026.9.7 (c074824)**, node 24.18.0
- macOS 26.6.2 (arm64), host "Rocky's home"
- Gateway flags: `--max-old-space-size=12288 --port 18789`
- ~843 stored sessions (837 for `main` agent), 27 subagent sessions

## Reproduction

1. Run the gateway with a large session store (hundreds of sessions, several >200k tokens).
2. Let it operate normally for ~1 hour (dashboard turns + occasional subagent spawns).
3. Watch RSS: it climbs ~23 MB/min and never returns to baseline. GC reclaims almost nothing (heap dropped only ~55 MB after a manual GC — the memory is **reachable**, not garbage).

## Evidence

Every gateway startup logs:

```
session-transcript.worker.js: started=2 retired=[]
```

The `retired=[]` is the smoking gun — the pool never retires these workers. Worker-heap inventory across the day:

| Time | instances | sizes (MB) | total |
|---|---|---|---|
| 08:29 | 5 | 86.8, 74.2, 35.0, 31.4, 27.1 | ~254 MB |
| 13:05 | 5 | 95.5, 73.6, 34.8, 32.1, 31.2 | ~267 MB |
| 14:07 (CRITICAL) | >=2 top-5 | **115.5**, 73.3 | — |

A "sticky pair" (~73 MB and ~86→115 MB) survives all day and grows monotonically (86.8 → 95.5 → 115.5 MB), matching the `97 MB → 115 MB` signature in the stability crash dumps.

Additionally, there were **5 `stop_shutdown_timeout` events today** (08:29, 11:33, 12:04, 12:51, 13:05) — the same workers block clean shutdown.

## Root cause (read-only source inspection)

In `dist/config/sessions/session-transcript.worker.js`:

- A module-level `historyDatabaseScopes` Map (line 10) retains `OpenClawAgentDatabaseReadOnlyScope` objects up to `MAX_RETAINED_HISTORY_DATABASES = 64` (line 9).
- Each retained scope holds an **open read-only SQLite connection** and an **enabled prepared-statement cache** (`enableNodeSqliteKyselyStatementCache`).
- Idle cleanup relies on an `.unref()`'d timer (in `OpenClawAgentDatabaseReadOnlyScope.touch()` / `closeIfIdle()`); under sustained transcript-hydration load the timer never fires and scopes are never closed.
- The worker pool itself never retires `session-transcript` workers (`retired` never populated), so each hydrated transcript stays pinned.

## Amplifier (config)

The model providers were configured with `contextWindow: 1000000` tokens. This causes the gateway to materialize/retain up to ~1M tokens of context per active session, which is what turns "a large session" into "100 MB of pinned transcript memory." Lowering to `262144` cuts per-session footprint ~4-8x and is the best available mitigation short of a code fix.

## Suggested fix direction

1. Retire idle `session-transcript` workers after an idle timeout (populate `retired`), releasing their retained scopes and SQLite connections.
2. Make `OpenClawAgentDatabaseReadOnlyScope` idle cleanup robust under load (the `.unref()`'d timer starves) — e.g. close scopes eagerly or use a real liveness check.
3. Consider not pinning prepared-statement caches on every retained read-only scope.

## Diagnostics

Diagnostics bundle (payload-free): `logs/support/openclaw-diagnostics-2026-10-01T12-33-47-457Z-42904.zip` (heap profile + stability events). Can attach on request.

```
openclaw gateway call diagnostics.heapProfile
openclaw gateway diagnostics export
```

Reported from a read-only investigation; no config/session changes were made as part of this report beyond the reversible `contextWindow` mitigation on the local host.

issues.body:
### Summary

Export the `session.stalled` and `session.long_running` diagnostic events from diagnostics-prometheus, because the gateway's "stalled session" warnings, the stall signal operators currently get, increment no Prometheus series.

### Problem to solve

The gateway logs `[diagnostic] stalled session:` for blocked tool calls and agent runs without progress. In this deployment the gateway log has 2,868 such records between 2026-10-04 00:00 and 2026-10-09 09:00 PDT, across 49 sessions (2,439 `reason=blocked_tool_call`, 429 `reason=active_work_without_progress`), with a longest logged age of 14,401 s. Over a separate Prometheus window (2026-10-04 22:00 PDT to 2026-10-09 09:07 PDT), a series query returns no series for `openclaw_session_stuck_total` or `openclaw_session_recovery_total`, and the exporter has no series for stalled or long-running sessions at all. An operator who alerts on the `stuck` or `recovery` names sees permanent silence while sessions are stalled for hours.

The cause is that the stalled log record is not a `session.stuck` event. `logSessionAttention` (src/logging/diagnostic.ts) labels the record from `classification.eventType` and emits one of three events: `session.long_running`, `session.stalled` or `session.stuck`. The stalled records above are all `session.stalled`. diagnostics-prometheus handles `session.stuck` and `session.recovery.*` but has no case for `session.stalled` or `session.long_running`, so those events are dropped. The HELP text of `openclaw_session_stuck_total` is "Stale session bookkeeping observations with no active work", a narrower condition (`queued_work_without_active_run` and the final fallback in `classifySessionAttention`), and the log has zero `stuck session:` records in the window. Every stalled record also carries `recovery=none` (the 2026.9.9 stalled classification is built with `recoveryEligible: false`), so no `session.recovery.*` event was emitted and the recovery counter stayed silent as well.

So the two metrics behave as designed, and the gap is that stalled and long-running sessions have no metric. diagnostics-otel also takes no action for these two events (`case "session.long_running": case "session.stalled": break;` at extensions/diagnostics-otel/src/service-events.ts:80-82 in 2026.9.9).

### Proposed solution

Add a handler in diagnostics-prometheus for the two events, alongside the existing `session.stuck` handler (extensions/diagnostics-prometheus/src/service-sessions.ts:101-118 on origin/main; service.ts:556-571 in 2026.9.9), with the bounded labels the event already carries:

- `openclaw_session_stalled_total{classification, reason, active_work_kind, state}` counter, and `openclaw_session_stalled_age_seconds` histogram with the same labels.
- `openclaw_session_long_running_total{reason, active_work_kind, state}` counter, and age histogram.

The age histograms need their own buckets. `store.histogram` already takes a `buckets` argument, but the default `DURATION_BUCKETS_SECONDS` ends at 600 s (the same ceiling reported for run durations in #167912). In this deployment 2,155 of the 2,868 stalled records (75%) had an age above 600 s, 908 above 3600 s, 413 above 7200 s, and the longest was 14,401 s, so with the default buckets three quarters of these observations would land in `+Inf`. Suggested age buckets: `30, 60, 120, 300, 600, 1800, 3600, 7200, 14400, 28800` s.

If the metric contract needs to start smaller, the counters alone close the main gap (an alertable signal that a session is stalled), and the age histograms can follow once the buckets are agreed.

`classification` is the closed set `blocked_tool_call | stalled_agent_run`. The existing stuck handler normalizes only `reason` with `normalizeDiagnosticValue` (its labels are `reason` and `state`); `activeWorkKind` needs the same treatment in the new handlers, as the recovery handler already does for `active_work_kind`. Do not add session id, session key or tool name labels (unbounded cardinality). The gateway re-logs a still-stalled session on a short interval (the records below are 30 s apart), so the counter counts observations, like `openclaw_session_stuck_total` does; a short docs sentence in docs/gateway/prometheus.md should say so and point out that `openclaw_session_stuck_total` covers only stale bookkeeping.

Intended alert shapes: `increase(openclaw_session_stalled_total{classification="blocked_tool_call"}[15m]) > 0`, grouped by `reason`; or a long-stall alert on a high bucket, for example `increase(openclaw_session_stalled_age_seconds_count[15m]) - increase(openclaw_session_stalled_age_seconds_bucket{le="3600"}[15m]) > 0` (stalled observations older than one hour). A histogram gives bucket counts and quantile estimates, not an exact maximum age.

### Alternatives considered

Widen `openclaw_session_stuck_total` to include stalled events: rejected, because its HELP text defines it as stale bookkeeping with no active work, and merging would change existing alert semantics. Scrape the gateway log for `stalled session:`: works, but not every operator ships gateway logs, and the Prometheus exporter is the documented operational surface. Rely on `openclaw_liveness_warning_total`: it counts event-loop liveness, not stalled sessions. Rely on `openclaw_session_state_total` and `openclaw_session_queue_depth`: they report session state and queue depth, not that active work has made no progress.

### Impact

Affected: operators who monitor the gateway through diagnostics-prometheus. Severity: medium, because a session blocked on a tool call for hours produces no stalled-session metric. Frequency: 2,868 stalled-session records on one gateway on each of the 6 calendar days from 2026-10-04 to 2026-10-09, 49 distinct sessions. Consequence: stalls surface only through log reading; alerts on `openclaw_session_stuck_total` never fire.

### Evidence/examples

Prometheus window: 2026-10-04 22:00 PDT to 2026-10-09 09:07 PDT (Prometheus 3.14.0 scraping `/api/diagnostics/prometheus` every 30 s). A range query on `/api/v1/series` over that window returns:

```
openclaw_session_stuck_total     -> {"status":"success","data":[]}
openclaw_session_recovery_total  -> {"status":"success","data":[]}
openclaw_session_state_total     -> 8 series (reasons such as message_completed, message_start; states idle, processing)
```

For comparison, `openclaw_session_state_total` and `openclaw_session_queue_depth` do have series, so scraping works. No series exists for any `openclaw_session_*stalled*` or `*long_running*` name.

Gateway log window (separate from the Prometheus window): 2026-10-04 00:00 PDT to 2026-10-09 09:00 PDT. 2,868 `stalled session:` records, all with `recovery=none`; 0 `stuck session:` and 0 `long-running session:` records. Consecutive records for one session, 30 s apart (age 553 s, 583 s, 613 s); across all sessions, 2,540 of 2,819 consecutive record pairs are 30 s apart:

```
2026-10-07T06:52:57.019-07:00 [diagnostic] stalled session: sessionId=5c7a9e98-5fe7-4705-9205-5fc87a17308c sessionKey=agent:main:dashboard:9e94621b-2693-4109-b8a8-ba836631bf23 state=processing age=553s queueDepth=0 reason=blocked_tool_call classification=blocked_tool_call activeWorkKind=tool_call lastProgress=tool:Bash:started lastProgressAge=129s activeTool=Bash activeToolCallId=toolu_01LxeFZKLAdU3AwZpRHf5y46 activeToolAge=129s recovery=none
2026-10-07T06:53:27.022-07:00 [diagnostic] stalled session: sessionId=5c7a9e98-5fe7-4705-9205-5fc87a17308c sessionKey=agent:main:dashboard:9e94621b-2693-4109-b8a8-ba836631bf23 state=processing age=583s queueDepth=0 reason=blocked_tool_call classification=blocked_tool_call activeWorkKind=tool_call lastProgress=tool:Bash:started lastProgressAge=159s activeTool=Bash activeToolCallId=toolu_01LxeFZKLAdU3AwZpRHf5y46 activeToolAge=159s recovery=none
```

An `active_work_without_progress` record (`classification=stalled_agent_run activeWorkKind=embedded_run`):

```

issues.body:
### Summary

Third-party channel plugins (e.g., WeCom) deliver replies successfully but never enter the official conversation_deliveries lifecycle, leaving no machine-readable outbound evidence chain for audit or recovery.


### Problem to solve

We operate multiple WeCom agents on OpenClaw 2026.8.2. Agent replies are delivered and visible in WeChat (with transcript timestamps), but `conversation_deliveries` stays at 0 rows — the official delivery lifecycle is completely bypassed.

This means:
- No machine-readable evidence distinguishing "locally accepted" from "channel acknowledged"
- No audit trail for outbound messages from third-party channels
- Manual visual verification is the only way to confirm delivery
- We cannot build automated recovery/retry without an official delivery record

Source inspection confirms: the WeCom plugin's `deliver` implementation calls `sendText` directly (logging only "reply delivered final") and never invokes `beginConversationDeliveryOperation` / `markQueued` / `markSent` / `markReplied`. Those operations are only triggered on core-owned routed channel turn paths (`messageSending: "channel-delivery"`), while the dispatcher path (`messageSending: "dispatcher"`) skips the entire lifecycle.

We need a supported integration point so third-party channel plugins can enter the official delivery lifecycle, or clear confirmation that `conversation_deliveries` is not intended to cover third-party channels (in which case we need an alternative official mechanism).


### Proposed solution

Provide a public delivery lifecycle hook/API that third-party channel plugins can invoke to enter the official `conversation_deliveries` lifecycle. Specifically:

1. A documented integration point (e.g., `channel.reportDeliveryOutcome(conversationId, messageId, status)`) that a plugin's `deliver` implementation can call after `sendText` succeeds.
2. The hook should support at minimum three states: `queued` → `sent` → `acked` (or equivalent), matching the existing core-owned channel turn lifecycle.
3. For channels whose send SDK returns only an error code (no platform message ID — e.g., WeCom `sendText` returns only `errcode`), allow a delivery record with state `sent` and no `platform_message_id` to serve as acceptable delivery evidence.
4. Alternatively (and preferably): route third-party channel replies through the same core-owned routed channel turn / durable delivery lifecycle used by native channels, so plugins don't need separate delivery reporting.

We are willing to contribute a PR for the WeCom plugin adapter once the official API surface is confirmed.


### Alternatives considered

- **Self-built receipt layer**: Write delivery records into `conversation_deliveries` outside the official store API. Rejected because it bypasses the official schema, risks corruption on schema migrations, and violates our principle of not writing to internal stores without a supported API.
- **Treat local send success as delivery**: Consider `errcode === 0` from WeCom `sendText` as sufficient evidence. Rejected because local acceptance ≠ channel acknowledgement; a message can be accepted locally but fail to reach the user (rate limits, account suspension, etc.). We need machine-readable evidence at the channel level.
- **Poll WeCom API for message status**: Query sent message status after delivery. Rejected because WeCom's API does not provide a reliable message-level delivery receipt endpoint for agent messages; this would add complexity without solving the evidence gap.


### Impact

- **Affected users/systems/channels**: All OpenClaw users who operate third-party channel plugins (WeCom, Feishu/Lark, Slack custom integrations, etc.) via the dispatcher path (`messageSending: "dispatcher"`). Any plugin using `dispatchReplyWithBufferedBlockDispatcher` with a custom `deliver` implementation is affected.
- **Severity**: Medium — blocks workflow. Without delivery evidence, operators cannot distinguish "message sent successfully" from "message accepted locally but never reached the user", making production monitoring, audit trails, and automated retry/recovery impossible for third-party channels.
- **Frequency**: Always / every outbound reply from third-party channels. This is a structural gap, not an edge case — every single WeCom agent reply bypasses the delivery lifecycle.
- **Consequence**: Extra manual work (visual verification in WeChat admin console per message), no automated audit trail, inability to build reliable recovery/retry logic, and potential silent delivery failures going undetected.


### Evidence/examples

**Environment**: OpenClaw 2026.8.2 (build 0965053), Windows, WeCom configured as third-party channel plugin (`wecom-openclaw-plugin`, npm-distributed).

**Minimal repro**:
1. Configure a WeCom agent channel and receive one real inbound message.
2. Let the agent reply; the reply is visible in WeChat (transcript has timestamp) and the plugin logs `[wecom-agent] reply delivered (final)`.
3. Query `conversation_deliveries` for that conversation: **0 rows**.

**Source code evidence** (from this build's `dist/`):
- Plugin deliver path: `core.channel.reply.dispatchReplyWithBufferedBlockDispatcher(...)` with plugin-supplied `deliver` → calls `sendText` directly, logs only `[wecom-agent] reply delivered (final)`
- Official delivery operations (`beginConversationDeliveryOperation`, `markQueued`, `markSent`, `markReplied`) are invoked only on `messageSending: "channel-delivery"` paths
- Dispatcher path uses `messageSending: "dispatcher"` → **skips entire delivery lifecycle**
- Key files: `dist/delivery-completion-*.js`, `dist/lifecycle-*.js`, `dist/dispatch-*.js`

**Note**: Inbound callback interruption (network issue) is a separate problem and intentionally excluded from this issue scope.


### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes, I plan to implement this myself

### Additional information

We are happy to provide additional diagnostics, test configurations, or participate in design discussions. Our team operates multiple WeCom agents in production and has done source-level inspection of the 2026.8.2 build to prepare this request.

Internal reference documents (local workspace, not linked):
- `PhaseA-3.3-送达确认层设计评估-20260906.md`
- `PhaseA-3.3-送达确认薄适配-风险评估与回滚方案-20260906.md`

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

In Slack, Feishu and Zalo Personal, a slash command with a multi-line argument reaches the command handler on one line. A `/btw` question followed by a pasted stack trace or code, or a multi-line `/loop` prompt, loses its line breaks and indentation before the model sees it: in Slack and Feishu in direct messages as well as in channels, in Zalo Personal when the message mentions the bot. https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/183606 fixed the same flattening in the core mention stripping; these three channel plugins flatten the command text before core sees it.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run a Gateway with a Slack account (HTTP events or Socket Mode) and an agent.
2. Send the bot one message, so the DM has a session.
3. Send this DM:

   ```text
   /btw QA-BTW-MULTILINE why does this fail?
     at first (a.ts:1)
       at second (b.ts:2)
   ```

4. Look at the `/btw` question in the model request.

The same happens in Feishu with the same text, and in a Zalo Personal group when the message mentions the bot before `/btw`.

### Expected behavior

The model receives the question as it was typed, with three lines and their indentation, as it does for the same text after https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/183606 in channels whose mention stripping runs in core.

### Actual behavior

The model receives `QA-BTW-MULTILINE why does this fail? at first (a.ts:1) at second (b.ts:2)`. Slack's `stripSlackMentionsForCommandDetection` (`extensions/slack/src/monitor/commands.ts`), Feishu's `normalizeFeishuCommandProbeBody` (`extensions/feishu/src/bot-content.ts`) and Zalo Personal's `stripOwnMentionsForCommandBody` (`extensions/zalouser/src/zalo-js.ts`) collapse every whitespace run to one space, and their result becomes the turn's command body.

### OpenClaw version

Source build at e68d5552923

### Operating system

Ubuntu 22.04

### Install method

Source build

### Model

Mock OpenAI provider (only to record the request; the bug is in the channel plugins)

### Provider / routing chain

Slack channel -> Gateway -> mock OpenAI provider

### Additional provider/model setup details

Isolated QA Gateway running the real Slack plugin against a local fake Slack API with signed Events API deliveries; the mock provider records each model request.

### Logs

```shell
model received the /btw question as "QA-BTW-MULTILINE why does this fail? at first (a.ts:1) at second (b.ts:2)"
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

The before and after captures are in the pull request.

### Impact and severity

- Affected: Slack, Feishu and Zalo Personal users who send slash commands with multi-line arguments (`/btw`, `/side`, `/loop`).
- Severity: the command runs, but pasted traces, code and lists arrive as one line, so the answer is about mangled input.
- Frequency: every multi-line slash command in Slack and Feishu, and every one that mentions the bot in Zalo Personal.
- Consequence: users have to avoid multi-line commands in these channels.

### Additional information

https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/183606 keeps whitespace for text that starts with `/` in core `stripMentions`. The Slack, Feishu and Zalo Personal command helpers still apply the old collapse.
