issues.body:
### Bug Description

For inference providers that authenticate with a dedicated HTTP header (e.g. a literal `api-key`
header, Azure-style or gateway routing tags configured via a named custom provider's
`extra_headers`), the main agent's chat calls succeed because the main client lifts the
provider's header block onto its requests. **Auxiliary session-title requests do not carry
those headers**, so title generation fails with an auth error (401/403) on every session:

```text
Title generation failed: Error code: 401 - {"error": {"message": "...missing required header 'api-key'..."}}
```

Sessions fall back to the provisional/derived instant title forever. This is the same failure
family as **#109595** ("named custom provider `extra_headers` dropped on aux clients"), which
was fixed in the _named-custom_ resolution branch but **not** in the _main-runtime-reuse_
branch — and main-runtime-reuse is exactly the branch `task="title_generation"` resolves
through.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure a named custom provider whose endpoint requires an `api-key` header, e.g. in
   `config.yaml`:
   ```yaml
   custom_providers:
     - name: my-gateway
       base_url: https://gateway.example.com/v1
       key_env: MY_GATEWAY_KEY
       extra_headers:
         api-key: '${MY_GATEWAY_API_KEY}' # required by the gateway; 401 without it
   model:
     provider: my-gateway
     model: some-model
   ```
2. Set it as the main runtime provider and start a fresh chat session (`hermes chat` / TUI).
3. Send any message. Main chat turns succeed (the header is lifted onto the main client).
4. Inspect `agent.log`: `Title generation failed: ... 401 ...` on the first exchange; the
   session keeps only the instant derived title (no LLM-generated title is ever stored).

### Expected Behavior

`call_llm(task="title_generation", main_runtime=...)` authenticates identically to the main
agent client for the same endpoint — the provider's `extra_headers`/`default_headers` block
(`api-key` included) is present on the title request, and titles are generated successfully.

### Actual Behavior

The title request is sent **without** the `api-key` header and the provider rejects it. The
auth failure is invisible except as a `WARNING` in `agent.log`; the UX symptom is only that
sessions never get real auto-titles.

### Affected Component

Agent Core (conversation loop, context compression, memory), CLI (interactive chat)

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

_No response_

### Debug Report

```shell
Report       https://dpaste.com/EDWRT2YRF
agent.log    https://dpaste.com/E3AF3NRQJ
gateway.log  https://dpaste.com/94K9UDYEP
gui.log      https://dpaste.com/7E9TFPWWH
update.log   https://dpaste.com/FP68BWVC2
```

### Operating System

Linux 6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2 (WSL)

### Python Version

Python 3.14.7

### Hermes Version

Hermes Agent v0.22.1 (2026.9.24) · stable · local `297552a9d646`

### Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)

```shell
WARNING Title generation failed: <auth error from provider — missing required header>


(`agent/title_generator.py:557`; stack trace at DEBUG under "Title generation traceback".)
```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

The auxiliary title call re-resolves a _fresh_ OpenAI client from a narrow runtime snapshot
that has no header field at all:

1. **Entry point** — `generate_title()` calls
   `call_llm(task="title_generation", ..., main_runtime=main_runtime)`
   (`agent/title_generator.py:514`).

2. **Snapshot producer** — the main runtime snapshot is built per turn at
   `agent/turn_context.py:542` via `auxiliary_client.set_runtime_main(...)`
   (`agent/auxiliary_client.py:2755-2784`). Its fields are exactly:
   `provider / requested_provider / model / base_url / api_key / api_mode / auth_mode /
session_id / cache_scope` (`_MAIN_RUNTIME_FIELDS`, `agent/auxiliary_client.py:3098-3101`;
   `agent/auxiliary_client.py:2770-2780`). **No `default_headers` / `extra_headers` field
   exists**, so the main client's provider header block cannot propagate.

3. **The dropping branch** — when the title call resolves through the main-runtime-reuse path
   inside `_resolve_custom_branch` (`agent/auxiliary_client.py:5093-5116`, the `#45472` fix
   that reuses `base_url` + `api_key` instead of re-resolving), the new `OpenAI(...)` client's
   headers come **only** from `_endpoint_default_headers(custom_base, provider, ...)`
   (`agent/auxiliary_client.py:2223-2244`), which knows about:
   - hardcoded host specials (Kimi / Copilot / NVIDIA NIM / xAI),
   - the _registry_ provider profile's `default_headers` (`_profile_default_headers`),
   - config `model.default_headers` / `model.extra_headers` (`_apply_user_default_headers`,
     `agent/auxiliary_client.py:874`).

   It does **not** consult the _named custom provider entry's_ `extra_headers` (where an
   `api-key` auth header typically lives), and nothing carries the live main client's
   header set. Result: the request ships with only `Authorization: Bearer <api_key>` and no
   `api-key` → provider 401/403.

4. **Fix asymmetry (why #109595 didn't cover this)** — the named-custom branch was fixed for
   the same class of bug: `_resolve_named_custom_branch` reads `normalize_extra_headers(
custom_entry.get("extra_headers"))` and applies it on every arm
   (`agent/auxiliary_client.py:5183`, `5215`, `5219` → `_named_custom_openai_wire_client`,
   `5135-5147`; Anthropic arm via `with_options(default_headers=...)`, `5209-5211`). The async
   rebuild also carries configured headers now (`agent/auxiliary_async_rebuild.py:36-42`).
   But those arms only fire when resolution _knows the provider name_; the title path's
   main-runtime-reuse branch (`5093`) is reached with a generic `custom`/alias provider
   identity and skips them entirely.

### Proposed Fix (optional)

**Primary — lift headers through the main-runtime snapshot:**

1. Add a `default_headers` field to `set_runtime_main()`
   (`agent/auxiliary_client.py:2755`), populated at the producer (`agent/turn_context.py:542`)
   from the live agent client's resolved header block (same composition
   `_named_custom_openai_wire_client` does: named-entry `extra_headers` merged over
   `_apply_user_default_headers`). Register it in `_MAIN_RUNTIME_FIELDS` /
   `_MAIN_RUNTIME_CONTEXT_FIELDS` (`3098-3101`) and preserve dicts in `_normalize_main_runtime`
   (`3104-3128`) like the existing callable-`api_key` special case.
2. In the main-runtime-reuse block of `_resolve_custom_branch` (`5093-5116`), merge
   `main_runtime["default_headers"]` into the `default_headers` passed to
   `_create_openai_client`.
3. Precedence must mirror the main client: host-special/profile headers <
   `model.default_headers`/`extra_headers` < named-entry `extra_headers` < per-request
   `extra_headers`. SECURITY: never log header values (consistent with existing helpers;
   `api-key` is already in `SECRET_HEADER_NAME_LIST`, `agent/redact.py:504`).
4. Ensure wrapped transports inherit on this branch too: `AnthropicAuxiliaryClient` via
   `with_options(default_headers=...)` (mirror `#109595` at `5211`), `CodexAuxiliaryClient` /
   `_wrap_transport` arms — and remember the Anthropic wire uses `x-api-key`, so the header
   name must not be blind-copied across wires.
5. Async parity: `_to_async_client` already copies `_custom_headers`
   (`agent/auxiliary_async_rebuild.py:36`), so new headers propagate automatically —
   confirm with one async-path test.

**Minimal alternative (smaller blast radius):** in the same branch, look up
`_get_named_custom_provider(requested_provider)` and apply
`normalize_extra_headers(entry["extra_headers"])` before falling back to
`_endpoint_default_headers`. Downside: fails when headers are minted per request (e.g. Entra
token refresh, `key_cmd`) rather than statically configured — the snapshot approach closes the
whole class.

### Are you willing to submit a PR for this?

- [ ] I'd like to fix this myself and submit a PR

issues.title: [Weixin] v0.22.5 destroys the valid context_token on -2/'prepare failed' and retries tokenless (iLink rejects tokenless sends) — the reply never lands
issues.body:
## Summary

On v0.22.5 the WeChat adapter **destroys the valid `context_token`** when iLink answers `-2 / "prepare failed"`, then retries the send **without** a token. iLink rejects tokenless sends unconditionally, so the message can never land no matter how many times it is retried. The failure is then reported as a *deterministic* `session not ready` error, which routes it away from the retry ladder and away from the delivery ledger's recovery path.

This is the **reply path**, not the proactive-push path — and it is what makes a long turn's answer go missing even though the user is actively typing in the chat.

Related: #135921 (outbound discarded when the peer reply window expires), #82502 (`-2 / "prepare failed"` misclassified as a rate limit), #94146 (live replies silently dropped after rate-limit incidents).

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.22.5 (release `v0.22.5`, 2026-10-23)
- Single `hermes-gateway` process, systemd `--user`
- Platform: WeChat personal account via the iLink bot adapter (`plugins/platforms/weixin/adapter.py`)
- One peer, one DM session

## The defect

### 1. `prepare failed` is treated as token expiry, and the token is *popped from the cache*

`plugins/platforms/weixin/adapter.py` (v0.22.5):

```python
def _is_stale_session_ret(ret, errcode, errmsg) -> bool:
    """Recognize stale-session variants of iLink's ``-2`` response, not real rate limits."""
    return (ret == RATE_LIMIT_ERRCODE or errcode == RATE_LIMIT_ERRCODE) and (errmsg or "").lower() in {
        "unknown error",
        "prepare failed",
    }

def _is_session_expired(resp, ret, errcode) -> bool:
    return SESSION_EXPIRED_ERRCODE in (ret, errcode) or _is_stale_session_ret(ret, errcode, resp.get("errmsg") or resp.get("msg"))
```

and then, in `_send_text_chunk`:

```python
if _is_session_expired(resp, ret, errcode) and not retried_without_token and context_token:
    retried_without_token, context_token = True, None
    self._token_store._cache.pop(self._token_store._key(self._account_id, chat_id), None)   # ← destroys the credential
    logger.warning("[%s] session expired for %s; retrying without context_token", self.name, _safe_id(chat_id))
    continue
```

The same `_cache.pop(...)` appears in the media path.

**`prepare failed` does not mean the token is stale.** It means iLink has not prepared a bot-initiated send for this peer — the peer has to message the bot again first. The held `context_token` is still the peer's latest token (it is refreshed on every inbound message) and remains a usable credential for the *next* real reply. Popping it from the cache means:

- the retry goes out tokenless, and iLink rejects tokenless sends → the message is dead;
- the cache no longer holds the peer's latest token, so the **next** inbound-driven reply is also degraded;
- the log line says `session expired`, which sends triage in the wrong direction entirely.

The token should be dropped **from this send only**, not from the cache.

### 2. The failure is reported as deterministic, which removes it from every recovery lane

```python
def _session_not_ready_error(ret, errcode, errmsg) -> RuntimeError:
    """The stale-session ``-2`` after the tokenless re-send is exhausted (or with no token to drop):
    iLink will not prepare a bot-initiated send until this peer messages the bot again. Deterministic,
    so it is neither retried nor fed to the rate-limit breaker (#80125). ..."""
    return RuntimeError(
        f"iLink sendmessage session not ready: ret={ret} errcode={errcode} errmsg={errmsg or 'unknown error'}"
        " — the user must send the bot a message first (or re-pair)")
```

Because the text contains no `retryable:` marker, `classify_send_error` in `gateway/platforms/base.py` does not classify it as transient, so it is neither retried nor handed to the deferred-redelivery lane — it is recorded as a hard failure and the content is gone.

### 3. Net effect on a real conversation

A turn's answer is produced normally, then the outbound send fails, and the reply never reaches the user even though they are actively in the chat. Observed on 2026-11-01:

```
2026-11-01 21:21:45,883 INFO  gateway.platforms.base: [Weixin] Sending response (190 chars) to o9cq804R…
2026-11-01 21:25:35,404 WARNING [Weixin] session expired for o9cq804R; retrying without context_token
2026-11-01 21:25:35,405 ERROR   [Weixin] send failed to=o9cq804R: iLink sendmessage session not ready: ret=-2 … prepare failed
```

and the delivery ledger records it as `failed`, never `delivered`:

```
state=abandoned  attempts=3  err=iLink sendmessage session not ready: ret=-2 errcode=None errmsg=prepare failed …
```

Over one evening: 36 deliveries abandoned with this error, 38 delivered.

## Reproduction

1. Send the bot a message (this refreshes the peer's `context_token`).
2. Let the peer window lapse, or simply let a long turn run past the window.
3. The next send hits `-2 / "prepare failed"`.
4. Observe: `session expired for …; retrying without context_token` → the cache is popped → the tokenless retry is rejected → `send failed … session not ready`.
5. `sqlite3 state.db "SELECT state,attempts,last_error FROM delivery_obligations WHERE platform='weixin'"` → `abandoned`, content gone.

## Suggested fix

1. **`_is_session_expired` must not classify `"prepare failed"` as token expiry.** Keep the token in the cache; drop it only from the send being retried. The cache is refreshed on every inbound message, so it always holds the peer's *latest* token — it is the last thing that should be thrown away.
2. **The `_session_not_ready_error` text should carry a `retryable:` marker** so `classify_send_error` returns `transient` rather than a hard failure. That routes the message into the deferred-redelivery lane (retry once the peer has actually written) instead of abandoning it. The existing docstring deliberately keeps the text free of the words "rate limit" so it does not feed the rate-limit breaker — a `retryable:` marker does not break that constraint.
3. **Back off and retry instead of breaking out.** The stale-session branch currently `break`s out of the send loop, ending the retry ladder on the first rejection.

A local patch implementing all three is in use on the deployment that produced this report; it has been verified end-to-end against the real `base._send_with_retry` path (28 assertions green, including a rate-limited chunk retrying with backoff instead of dropping). The decisive log line changes from a dropped message to:

```
[Weixin] Send failed (attempt 1/2, retrying in 2.4s): iLink sendmessage rate limited
```

Happy to open a PR with the patch if that is useful — it is small and self-contained (`_is_session_expired`, `_session_not_ready_error`, and the stale-session branch in `_send_text_chunk`, plus the `_RETRYABLE_ERROR_PATTERNS` table in `gateway/platforms/base.py`).

issues.body:
## Summary

A cron job's tool call to a remote MCP server's function (verified with Composio, `https://connect.composio.dev/mcp`) intermittently and *permanently* disappears from the session's model-facing tool list partway through — even though `hermes mcp test <server>` confirms the connection and the tool are completely healthy at the same time. The agent then retries the same call repeatedly instead of recognizing the tool is gone, burning many turns and a rapidly growing context before either hitting `max_turns` or being killed manually.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent, `main @ b6b53c69` (2026-09-12), git install
- Ubuntu, Python 3.11.15
- Reproduced on a cron job (`cron.scheduler --external-worker-file`) using an HTTP-transport MCP server (Composio) configured in `config.yaml` under `mcp_servers`

## Symptom (real incident, today)

A cron job normally completing in 20s–9min ran for 10+ minutes and 36+ model API calls, input context climbing past 60K tokens, repeatedly calling the same remote-sandbox MCP tool. Along the way it hit:
- A `tool_call` wrapper argument-validation error stripping required parameters from a `COMPOSIO_MULTI_EXECUTE_TOOL` call
- `Tool 'mcp__composio__COMPOSIO_MULTI_EXECUTE_TOOL' does not exist. Available tools: <list without it>` — despite `tool_search` reporting the tool as available moments earlier

I killed the stuck worker process manually. Immediately after, `hermes mcp test composio` on the *same profile* connected in 3.4s and cleanly discovered all 7 tools, including the one the session claimed didn't exist. This is not a Composio-side outage — the tool genuinely exists, in the same profile, seconds later.

This is the **third** occurrence of the identical failure combination in this install (previous ones dated 2026-09-08 and 2026-09-12 in our own operational notes) — always on this exact cron job, always after the tool worked at least once earlier in the same run.

## What I ruled out

- **Not a broken/expired Composio connection.** `hermes mcp test <server>` immediately after the incident connects and lists tools cleanly.
- **Not a config problem.** The server is declared once in `config.yaml` under `mcp_servers` and doesn't change mid-run.

## Suspected mechanism (traced, not fully confirmed)

`model_tools.py`'s `get_tool_definitions()` memoizes its result in a module-level `_tool_defs_cache`, keyed only on `(enabled_toolsets, disabled_toolsets, skip_tool_search_assembly)`, whenever `quiet_mode=True` (the path cron jobs use). This cache has no TTL and nothing re-validates it against current MCP registry/connection state — it's invalidated only by an explicit full `_clear_tool_defs_cache()` call or LRU eviction under memory pressure.

`cron/scheduler.py`'s `_init_cron_mcp_tools()` explicitly calls `discover_mcp_tools()` *before* constructing `AIAgent`, specifically to avoid a startup race (per its own comment: "cron jobs never saw any MCP tools" before this was added — issue #4219). But if registering an HTTP-transport MCP server (`tools/mcp_tool_discovery.py` → `tools/mcp_tool_registration.py`) is asynchronous or eventually-consistent under the hood, it's possible for the *first* `get_tool_definitions(quiet_mode=True)` call in the process to run before that server's tools are fully registered in `tools.registry`. That first (incomplete) result then gets cached under the toolset-selection key and served for the *rest of the process's life* — even after the server finishes connecting and its tools become available in the registry moments later.

Separately, `tools/mcp_tool_registration.py`'s `_register_connected_into_current_scope()` treats a server as "stale" (and removes this profile's scope registration via `_remove_server_scope`) whenever `getattr(server, "session", None) is None` at check time. For a remote HTTP MCP transport, `.session` can plausibly be transiently `None` during a normal reconnect/keepalive cycle — if that staleness check runs during such a window, it looks indistinguishable from a genuinely dead server and the profile's tools get evicted, with nothing re-adding them once the connection recovers (since nothing re-invalidates `_tool_defs_cache` on recovery either).

Both paths converge on the same observable symptom: a real, working MCP tool silently and permanently vanishes from one session's active tool surface.

## Impact

- Real API/compute cost: a stuck cron job burns dozens of retried calls against a growing context before it's caught.
- No user-facing error until the agent itself notices and either gives up or (as in our case) needs to be killed manually.
- Recurs on a roughly-weekly cadence for the same job in our install; likely affects any long-running session (cron or otherwise) using a remote/HTTP MCP server.

## Workaround in use

Delegating the MCP-dependent step to a fresh subagent (`delegate_task`) reliably works — subagents get a fresh tool surface and the same MCP function is present and callable there. This is a mitigation, not a fix, and costs an extra round-trip.

## Suggested fix directions

1. Don't cache `get_tool_definitions()` results until MCP server registration for that process/session has fully settled (or invalidate the cache once any pending MCP connection resolves after the first cache fill).
2. Make the staleness check in `_register_connected_into_current_scope()` tolerant of a transient `session is None` (e.g. require it to persist across N consecutive checks, or use a positive "connecting" state rather than treating "not yet connected" the same as "disconnected").
3. At minimum, surface a clear, distinguishable error when a tool is dropped from the surface mid-session (vs. the current generic "does not exist"), so an agent can reliably detect this specific condition and pivot to the subagent workaround immediately instead of retrying blind.

Happy to provide more detail/logs if useful — this hit us in production three times so I have execution traces for all three occurrences.

issues.title: [Weixin] A gateway restart mid-turn pauses the conversation's FIFO for as long as the user doesn't run /discard — 18h of silence, later messages get no reply at all
issues.body:
## Summary

On WeChat, a gateway restart that interrupts an in-flight turn leaves the **whole conversation's FIFO paused for as long as the user does not notice and run `/discard`**. Every message the user sends in the meantime is committed to the durable queue but **never answered** — no reply, no error, no heartbeat. Measured on a personal deployment: **18 h 23 min of total silence across 11 messages**, ending only when the user happened to trigger a session reset themselves.

This is not the WeChat transport failing. It is the messaging-platform UX of the `unknown_execution` pause, and it is invisible on every platform that has its own UI affordance for a lost turn (Desktop shows a "Turn lost during restart" row; TUI shows a queue). On WeChat the user has **no** such affordance — only a one-shot text notice that is easy to miss.

Related but distinct: #135921 (outbound message discarded when the peer reply window expires — the transport side), #147343 (Desktop: `/discard` leaves the session silently idle), #147634 (RFC: settling work fenced `unknown`).

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.22.5 (release `v0.22.5`, 2026-10-23)
- Single `hermes-gateway` process, systemd `--user`, `hermes-gateway.service`
- Platform: WeChat personal account via the iLink bot adapter (`plugins/platforms/weixin/adapter.py`)
- One peer, one DM session

## What happened (2026-11-01, 02:47 → 21:10 CST)

1. `02:55:05` — the gateway was restarted (`Received SIGTERM as a planned gateway stop`). A turn was in flight at that moment.
2. On the next start the in-flight admission was recovered as `status='unknown'` in `session_admissions`, and the session's FIFO was fenced:

```
2026-11-01 02:56:22,329 INFO gateway.run_runtime: Native session startup recovery
    20260819_092235_e8350b12 (/home/ubuntu/.hermes): unknown_execution
2026-11-01 15:59:16,592 WARNING gateway.session_authority: Session 20260819_092235_e8350b12 paused: unknown_execution
```

3. From that moment **every** inbound message was committed to the queue and **none of them ran**. The user sent 11 messages over 18 h 23 min:

```
seq  status   timestamp                text
27   unknown  2026-11-01T02:47:00Z     又停下了？你说看字节结构之后我就没收到消息了
28   queued   2026-11-01T15:59:16Z     总结一下：<video link>
29   queued   2026-11-01T16:01:08Z     那不想用微信了，居然对peer有限制
30   queued   2026-11-01T18:13:07Z     then
31   queued   2026-11-01T19:49:51Z     ？
32   queued   2026-11-01T19:50:07Z     你搞坏了？
33   queued   2026-11-01T20:50:56Z     收到了吗
34   queued   2026-11-01T20:53:11Z     /
35   queued   2026-11-01T21:05:09Z     /
36   queued   2026-11-01T21:10:01Z     hi
37   queued   2026-11-01T21:10:32Z     我一直收不到你的消息！
```

The messages were **not lost** — the original text is recoverable from `session_admissions.payload_json` → `native_text_v1.text` — but the user got no answer and no indication of why.

4. The only feedback the user received was **two** copies of this notice, hours apart:

```
⏸️ This conversation is paused: a previous turn did not finish when Hermes restarted,
and only you know whether to send it again. Your message is saved. Send /discard to drop
the lost turn and continue (it is not re-run), or /reset to start a fresh conversation.
```

5. `21:10:48` — a `session_reset` happened (triggered from the chat). The conversation recovered immediately.

## Why the platform matters

`gateway/session_ingress.py::pause_notice()` fires **once per pause episode**:

```python
live = authority.sessions[ref.session_id]
if live.pause_notified:
    return None          # ← every later message on this pause gets NO reply at all
live.pause_notified = True
```

So after the first notice, messages 2…N are *admitted silently* — the user sends "？", "你搞坏了？", "收到了吗" and gets **nothing**. From the user's side that is indistinguishable from the bot being dead, and it is exactly what produced "我一直收不到你的消息！".

The notice also asks the user to run `/discard` — a command that exists and is wired up on WeChat (`_PLAIN_COMMANDS` in `gateway/run_busy.py` includes `discard`), but which a messaging user has no reason to know about, and which is the **only** thing standing between them and an unbounded outage.

Two aggravating factors specific to messaging platforms:

- **The notice is itself a proactive push.** It goes out through the ordinary reply path, but on WeChat the peer reply window may already be closed, in which case the notice itself is discarded (#135921). The user then gets *nothing at all* — not even the one hint.
- **After the pause, the queued messages are unreachable.** Once the conversation is reset, the old session's rows are orphaned: `hermes sessions discard <old-session> --yes` → `Error: session_superseded`. The 11 messages above could only be recovered by reading `state.db` directly.

## Reproduction

1. Start a turn on a messaging platform (WeChat).
2. Kill the gateway mid-turn (`SIGTERM`).
3. Send the bot a message. Observe `Session <id> paused: unknown_execution` and one `⏸️` notice.
4. Send 3–4 more messages. Observe: **no replies at all**, no further notices.
5. `sqlite3 state.db "SELECT seq,status,text FROM session_admissions WHERE status='queued'"` → the messages are queued, never run.

## Suggested direction

Three independent angles, any one of which would have prevented this 18-hour outage:

1. **Re-notify on a paused FIFO.** `pause_notified` currently latches for the whole episode. A periodic or threshold-based re-notice (e.g. every N minutes, or every Nth admitted message) would keep the user informed without spamming. Today only the first message gets any feedback at all.
2. **Make the pause self-healing or visible.** Either auto-settle an `unknown` turn after a grace period on messaging platforms (the turn is not replayed — the same fenced resolution `/discard` uses), or surface "this conversation has been paused for N hours" in a way the user can see without knowing the internal command.
3. **Don't strand the queued messages on reset.** When a session is reset while rows are still `queued`, the user loses those messages permanently (`session_superseded`). The text is still in `state.db`; it should be surfaced (or re-queued into the new session) rather than orphaned.

Note the fenced-`unknown` design itself is correct and should stay — replaying a turn whose side effects may have run is worse. The gap is entirely in the messaging-platform UX and in the recovery path.

issues.title: [Bug]: Shared browser profile refused forever after a container recreate: stale SingletonLock + retained launch record read as "a Chromium in another environment"
issues.body:
> *Drafted with an AI assistant; posted by the account owner.*

### Bug Description

Recreate a container (`docker compose up -d` after an image bump, or `docker compose down/up`) while its Bot Screen Chromium is running. The persistent profile on the volume keeps:

- `SingletonLock -> <hostname>-<pid>` (plus `SingletonCookie`, `SingletonSocket`)
- `DevToolsActivePort`, which names the old browser's `/devtools/browser/<id>`
- the old container's launch record `<digest16>-<pid>-n<oldns>.json`, in `<gateway lock dir>/browser-shared-profiles/<digest32>/`, also on the volume

In the new container, every `browser_*` / `browser_exec` call on that profile fails with:

```
The browser profile /opt/data/bot-desktop/browser-profile is in use by a Chromium in another environment (a container or the host) that this process can neither reach nor verify, so Hermes will not start a second browser on it. ...
```

No Chromium is running anywhere. It never recovers by itself. After one fleet rollout, 7 of our 10 agents were stuck like this until someone deleted `Singleton*` by hand.

### Why

`_start_shared` (`tools/browser_launcher.py:527`) asks `_foreign_holder` (`:316`) first:

```python
if _pid_alive(pid) and _cmdline_names_dir(pid, user_data_dir):
    return None
if host != socket.gethostname() or _foreign_record_names(user_data_dir, pid):
    return pid
```

Compose pins `hostname:`, so the hostname matches. The old pid is not a live Chromium in the new PID namespace. Up to here this is the "stale lock of this environment" case, where a launch would take over the lock (as Chromium itself would).

But `_foreign_record_names` (`:333`) finds the retained record. Its pid matches, `same_namespace(record)` is False because the pid-namespace inode changed, the profile matches, and `record["devtools"]` equals the path in the stale `DevToolsActivePort`. So the lock counts as foreign. `_attach_foreign` then probes the endpoint, gets no answer, and returns None. `_start_shared` returns `_foreign_unreachable`. Nothing ever removes the record or the lock: `_bind_launch_record` says "Records of earlier containers and boots are kept" (`:458`).

The deciding fact here is "a record from another PID namespace exists". That proves a browser existed there once. It does not prove one is alive now.

### Steps to Reproduce

Minimal, no Docker needed. Run from a checkout of `main` (557254faa2) with `ruamel.yaml psutil requests pyyaml` installed:

```python
import json, os, socket, tempfile
from pathlib import Path
work = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
os.environ["HERMES_GATEWAY_LOCK_DIR"] = str(work / "locks")
os.environ["HERMES_HOME"] = str(work / "home")
from tools import browser_launcher as bl

udd = work / "browser-profile"; udd.mkdir()
dead_pid = 3037                                   # the old container's Chromium; nothing runs it here
os.symlink(f"{socket.gethostname()}-{dead_pid}", udd / "SingletonLock")
path = "/devtools/browser/0b9f4c1e-dead-4bad-8c0d-000000000000"
(udd / "DevToolsActivePort").write_text(f"9\n{path}\n")
state = bl._shared_state_dir(str(udd))
(state / f"{bl._profile_digest(str(udd))[:16]}-{dead_pid}-n000000000000.json").write_text(json.dumps({
    "owner_pid": 1, "owner_start_time": 1, "pid": dead_pid, "start_time": 1, "user_data_dir": str(udd),
    "home_key": "x", "ephemeral": False, "ns": "4026532999:old", "devtools": path}))

print(bl._foreign_holder(str(udd)))               # -> 3037
print(bl._start_shared("k", "/bin/false", str(udd), "x", None, headed=False, extra_args=(), env=None,
                       timeout=5, sandbox_bypass=True)[1])   # -> "... in use by a Chromium in another environment ..."
```

Delete the record file and `_foreign_holder` returns `None`, so the next launch takes over the stale lock. The retained record alone turns a stale lock into a permanent refusal.

In Docker: start a container with a persistent `/opt/data` and a pinned `hostname:`, run any `browser_exec` so the shared-profile Chromium starts, run `docker compose up -d --force-recreate`, then run `browser_exec` again.

### Expected Behavior

When the browser a record names is gone, the record and the lock are stale. The next launch takes over the profile, as it does after a crash in the same environment.

### Actual Behavior

The profile is refused permanently. The error text suggests deleting `SingletonLock`, but an agent cannot safely tell whether a browser still runs "elsewhere", so in practice a human has to step in.

### Proposed Fix

Decide a record's liveness from a lock the kernel holds, not from the record existing. This is the pattern of #144816, and it fixes the same class of bug as #123187.

1. **Liveness lock passed to Chromium.** At launch (`_spawn`, `:430`), open `<state>/<record-stem>.alive`, take `flock(LOCK_SH)`, and pass the fd to Chromium via `pass_fds`. The open file description lives as long as the Chromium process does, even after its launcher exits. It is released when the container dies, whatever namespace it was in. flock on a shared bind mount works across containers on one kernel.
2. **`_foreign_record_names` counts a record only while that lock is held.** If `flock(LOCK_EX | LOCK_NB)` on the record's `.alive` file succeeds, the browser is gone. Remove the record and treat the `SingletonLock` as stale (a launch takes it over). If the lock is held, keep today's behaviour: attach through the endpoint, or refuse.
3. **Records from another boot are always stale.** `ns_identity()` already includes the kernel boot id. A record with a different boot id names a browser that cannot be alive. Prune it at the same point. This alone fixes the host-reboot variant, though not container recreate.
4. **Old records with no `.alive` file:** keep the current conservative answer unless the hostname matches, no live local process has `--user-data-dir=<dir>` in its argv, and the DevTools endpoint does not answer. Then treat the record as stale. This lets profiles already stuck before the upgrade recover once.

Case (1)/(2) needs a test: the record's owner dies → the next `_start_shared` launches. Case (4) needs one too: a record from another live namespace whose lock is held → it is still refused or attached, never launched over.

### Workaround (what we do today)

As the profile's UID inside the new container: if no process has `--user-data-dir=<profile>` in its argv, delete `<profile>/SingletonLock`, `SingletonCookie` and `SingletonSocket`. The next browser call launches normally. Removing the lock alone is enough, because `_foreign_holder` returns `None` with no lock, but removing all three is the clean state.

### Environment

Seen live on a fork of Hermes Agent; the repro above runs on upstream `main` 557254faa2. Docker Compose with persistent `/opt/data` and a pinned `hostname:`, Debian Chromium 156, Bot Screen on Xvnc.

prs.title: Capabilities switches now say On/Off instead of the confusing Enable/Disable
prs.body:
The switches on the Capabilities page (Skills, Tools, Plugins) had a caption naming what a click would do, so a switch that was ON said "Disable" and an OFF one said "Enable". People read that word as the switch's current state and got it backwards; now the caption says what the switch is: "On" or "Off".

Reported on X by @theSammyK ("change the labels on the enable/disable slider switches from a verb to a state").

## What changes

| Switch | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| lit (enabled) | Disable | On |
| dark (disabled) | Enable | Off |
| non-English UI | English "Disable"/"Enable" (never translated) | localized `common.on`/`common.off` (An/Aus, Activado/Desactivado, オン/オフ, ...) |

- `CatalogSwitch` (the one component behind every Capabilities switch, including the Tools "all" toggle) renders `t.common.on` / `t.common.off`, the same On/Off-beside-the-switch pattern Windows Settings uses. The two captions still share one grid cell, so the switch never shifts when it flips.
- `settings.plugins.enable` / `settings.plugins.disable` had no other caller and no translation in any locale (both listed for all 8 overlays in `overlay-gaps.json`); removed with their gap entries.
- Screen-reader names are unchanged (each switch keeps its own `aria-label`).

## Live check

Real Electron app on a private Xvfb, real gateway in a scratch home, Capabilities, then Tools, with Code Execution and Kanban switched off. Same running instance for both legs (main leg = `origin/main` copies of the two changed files hot-swapped in).

main: lit switches say "Disable", off ones say "Enable"

![main](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/teknium1/7671c3ae2334a3d99a093db7a1983337/raw/main-tools-crop.png)

this PR: lit switches say "On", off ones say "Off"

![head](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/teknium1/7671c3ae2334a3d99a093db7a1983337/raw/head-tools-crop.png)

DOM readback of the visible captions, first four Tools cards: main `Disable,Enable,Disable,Disable`, head `On,Off,On,On` (paired with `aria-checked` true/false/true/true). Skills tab featured card: head `On`.

## Verification

- `npm run check:lint` (typecheck + eslint) in `apps/desktop`: 0 errors.
- `npx vitest run src/app/capabilities src/i18n`: 41 files, 224 tests passed (includes the overlay-completeness/gap tests).
- `scripts/check --only health`: 0 blocking.

prs.title: perf: token-estimate memo is an LRU with a 64 MiB idle budget; active conversations never evicted
prs.body:
Hermes saves a token count for every message it has measured, so it doesn't measure the same text twice, and to do that it keeps the text in memory. Before this PR it threw away the oldest 4,096 saved counts first, even when they belonged to a conversation still running, and the memory held had no size limit. Now it throws away the counts nobody has used for the longest time and aims to stay under 64 MiB. It never throws away a count used in the last minute. A running conversation, even one bigger than 64 MiB on its own, keeps all its saved counts, and dead sessions' text leaves memory.

**Outcome:** the per-message token-estimate memo (`_MSG_TOKENS_CACHE`) is an LRU with a retained-bytes budget and an entry backstop. Only idle entries are evicted, so no running conversation ever loses its hits, whatever its size or however many others run beside it.

## Changes
- The memo moves to `agent/model_metadata_token_memo.py` as an `OrderedDict`. A hit calls `move_to_end`, and inserts evict from the front. A plain-dict FIFO rescans its deleted slots on every eviction: 7.9 µs per eviction at 65k entries, against 0.19 µs for `OrderedDict.popitem`.
- Two bounds, least recently used first:
  - **Retained bytes, 64 MiB.** This counts pinned string bytes plus ~120 B of fingerprint structure per string leaf. A real 1M-token history retains about 9 MB; the estimate reads 11.7 MB.
  - **65,536 entries** as a backstop. The old bound was 4,096 entries.
- **Active entries are never evicted.** Each lookup stamps its entry. Both bounds stop at the first least-recently-used entry looked up within the last 60 s (`_ACTIVE_WINDOW_S`), because every entry behind it is more recent. A conversation larger than the budget overshoots it while it runs instead of missing on every message. The first insert after that conversation goes idle sheds the overshoot. Protected entries pin strings the running conversation holds anyway, so the overshoot costs only fingerprint structure.
  - After an idle gap over 60 s (for example a long tool call while other traffic fills the budget), a conversation recomputes the evicted part once. That costs about the same as its first estimate (≤ ~130 ms for 1M tokens), at most ~0.2% of the gap, and the next pass hits again.
  - The stamp lives on the pins list (`MemoPins`, a `list` subclass with one slot). The `(pins, text, images)` entry shape and every existing reader are unchanged.
- Insert, evict and `forget_message_token_memo` share one lock, so the byte count stays exact across gateway worker threads. The hit path takes no lock.
- Eviction never changes an estimate: a later lookup recomputes the same value.

## Measured
The bench is the real `estimate_messages_tokens_rough`, run on a fresh shallow copy each pass, as the conversation-loop preflight does. "Real 1M history" means 2,403 message rows from a real long session, 1.10M estimated tokens. "Image-heavy" means a synthetic 505-message history with 80 distinct ~1.2 MB base64 image data URLs (96 MB of image strings, 97 MB retained), above the 64 MiB budget. Each pass appends one message.

The legs run in one session on the same host:
- base: `e99ab8c7`, FIFO 4,096.
- previous head: `7faacc6e`, this PR's LRU without active protection.
- head: this push.
- uncapped: head with both bounds disabled.

The host was under load (load average ~50 to 59), so absolute ms are about 2× the earlier quiet-host run. Compare legs within a row.

| Scenario | base (FIFO 4,096) | previous head (LRU, 64 MiB) | **head (LRU, 64 MiB, active protected)** | uncapped |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Image-heavy, 96 MB, over the budget: ms per estimate, messages recomputed per pass** | 1.8 / 1.6 ms, 1 | **17.9 / 17.9 ms, 496 of 505 (thrash)** | **2.2 / 2.1 ms, 1** | 2.1 / 2.1 ms, 1 |
| Same, retained estimate at the end | (no byte bound) | 66.7 MB (budget) | 97.1 MB while active, shed when idle | 97.1 MB |
| Real 1M history, steady ms/estimate (hit rate) | 13.6 ms (100%) | 17.2 ms (100%) | 16.3 ms (100%) | 18.0 ms (100%) |
| **Two real 1M conversations interleaving** | **129.6 ms, 0% hits** | 15.4 ms, 100% | **17.8 ms, 100%** | 17.1 ms, 100% |
| Running 1M conversation while 200 dead sessions stream through: its hit rate | 91% | 100% | 100% | 100% |
| Same, unique text pinned at the end, dead sessions paced 5 s apart | 14.9 MB (4,096 entries, any size) | 44.2 MB (retained 67.0 = budget) | **44.2 MB (retained 67.0 = budget)** | 137 MB, growing |
| Same, bench speed (200 dead sessions in ~4 s, all within 60 s) | 14.9 MB | 44.2 MB | 137 MB until they idle 60 s | 137 MB |
| Memo structure per entry (tracemalloc) | 1,912 B | 1,958 B | 1,990 B | – |

- Base does not thrash on the image row: it bounds 4,096 entries, not bytes, so 505 large entries fit. That is the same reason base let 4,096 large tool outputs pin gigabytes. The previous head bounded the bytes but turned that row into a miss on every message. Head keeps the byte bound for idle memory and keeps base's hit rate for the running conversation.
- The single-conversation ms are within run-to-run noise on this host: the uncapped and capped legs of the same tree differ by more than the trees do.
- At bench speed every dead session counts as active for 60 s, so the unpaced churn row holds them until they idle. Real dead sessions also go through `close()`, which already drops their entries (`forget_message_token_memo`).

**Live gateway**, from the previous head: a real `gateway run --force` under a scratch home, real Nous turns on `google/gemini-3.8-flash`, local sessions over the canonical client path.
- Base, after 7 sessions closed and 2 min idle: 56 entries. It held 14 pinned copies of the same ~20 KB system-prompt-plus-ephemeral string, 2 per session, still there after idle eviction.
- Head with the budget scaled to 150 KB: 21 entries, 4 copies, 0.147 MB retained.
- Head at the real budget: same shape as base. The budget is far away at that scale.

This push changes eviction only for entries looked up within 60 s, so those live numbers stand. Billed: $0.25 total, previous live legs only; this push made no model calls.

## Composes with #146788
Teammate PR #146788 (`perf/token-memo-request-time-pins`) releases the per-request string copies the memo pins. It also changes the entry shape to value-keyed. The two PRs touch the same memo section, so whichever lands second gets rebased onto the other. After #146788 lands, this PR's byte accounting (`_entry_bytes`) counts the key strings that #146788 keeps in the key instead of the pins list. The bounds, the LRU order and the active-window protection carry over unchanged.

## Tests
`tests/agent/test_token_memo_lru_budget.py` holds 3 invariants:
- Two 2,500-message conversations interleaving keep 100% hits.
- With 10 dead 1 MB bodies past a 3.5 MB budget, each going idle before the next arrives, the running message stays pinned and at most 3 dead bodies remain. Estimates are unchanged.
- A 5,000-message conversation larger than both bounds (1 MB, 1,000 entries) computes only each pass's new message. Once it goes idle, the next insert sheds the memo back under both bounds.

Red checks:
- On base all three fail: `assert 15000 == 0`, `assert 10 <= 3`, `assert 15006 == 3`.
- On the previous head the third fails with `assert 15006 == 3`.

These existing suites pass unmodified (128 passed): `test_token_memo_release_on_close.py`, `test_cursor_optimizations_parity.py`, `test_model_metadata.py`. Every test file that references the memo or `estimate_messages_tokens_rough` (34 files) passes: 590 passed, 0 failed, on the rebased head. `scripts/check` passes.

prs.title: perf: import run_agent defers built-in tool modules, cron and the gateway adapter stack
prs.body:
`import run_agent`, which every CLI, TUI, desktop-backend and gateway process pays, no longer imports the built-in tool modules, the cron scheduler or the gateway adapter stack. Tool schemas and system-prompt bytes are unchanged.

## Numbers

Same machine (Apple Silicon, Python 3.14), empty temp `HERMES_HOME`, median of 5 fresh interpreters, base = parent commit:

| `import run_agent` | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| warm bytecode (normal installs after first run) | 0.58 s, 117 MB peak RSS | **0.45 s, 103 MB** |
| no project `.pyc` (`PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1`, fresh checkout) | 1.67 s, 141 MB | 1.14 s, 126 MB |
| modules in `sys.modules` | 1333 | 1125 |
| Hermes modules executed | 643 | 447 |
| `gateway.*` / `cron.*` / `tools.*` modules | 27 / 23 / 174 | 10 / 0 / 36 |

About the second row: an earlier 1.7–2.3 s figure was measured in a shell that exports `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1`. Without bytecode, `builtins.compile` alone took ~1.2 s of that, recompiling ~800 modules on every run. The warm row is what users get.

Building the first `AIAgent(enabled_toolsets=["hermes-cli"])` imports 23 of the 42 tool modules and leaves the other 19 unimported (discord, feishu, yuanbao, kanban, the GUI-only tools, …). Import plus that first agent goes from 1.05 s to 1.03 s and from 168 MB to 165 MB peak. That toolset genuinely needs most of the heavy modules, so for this path most of the import saving moves into the agent build. The interactive CLI banner calls `check_tool_availability()`, which reads the whole registry, so a plain `hermes` session still imports every tool module at startup.

## What changed

**Tool discovery is lazy** (`tools/registry.py`, `model_tools.py`)
- `defer_builtin_tools()` indexes each `tools/*.py` / `tools/<pkg>/tool.py` that registers at import: its tool names and toolsets are read from source with `ast`, covering literal `registry.register(...)` calls and module-level `for` loops over literal tables (discord, feishu_drive, kanban, xai_video, yuanbao). The index is cached in the existing `tool_discovery_cache.json` under the same mtime/size key.
- The registry imports a module the first time a lookup needs one of its tools or toolsets: `get_entry`/`dispatch` by name, `get_definitions` for the requested names, `get_tool_names_for_toolset` for a toolset. Whole-registry reads (`get_all_entries`, `get_tool_to_toolset_map`, `check_tool_availability`, …) import everything, and `discover_builtin_tools()` still imports everything up front for callers that read the registry directly.
- `register()`, `deregister()` and `snapshot_registration()` first import the built-in a name belongs to. A plugin override therefore still meets the built-in it replaces: the shadow and override checks run against it, and the plugin ledger's restore point is the built-in entry rather than an empty slot.
- **Profile scope:** a deferred import runs in an empty `contextvars.Context`, so its import-time values bind the launch profile, as boot-time discovery did. They never bind the served profile whose turn first needed the tool.
- **Threading:** imports never run under the registry `_lock`. A lookup racing another thread's import of the same module waits on Python's module lock and then sees the registrations. A failed import is logged once with its traceback and not retried by lookups, matching eager discovery's single attempt.
- A module whose registrations can't be read statically is imported whenever the index can't rule it out. No such module exists today, and a test enforces that.
- `model_tools.TOOL_TO_TOOLSET_MAP` and `TOOLSET_REQUIREMENTS` are built on first access via module `__getattr__`.
- `tool_search_catalog.hidden_declared_sources()` reads only `mcp-*` entries through the new `registry.get_entries_for_toolset_prefix()`, instead of loading every entry to filter for them.

**Gateway chain** (`gateway/platforms/__init__.py`)
- The bundled `a2a` plugin's client tools import `gateway.platforms._shared` in every CLI process. That module is dependency-light by design, but the package `__init__` eagerly imported `base` and `event`, which pulled in sessions and ~17 more gateway modules. The exports now resolve on first use, as `gateway/__init__.py` already does; no caller uses the package-level names.

**Cron chain**
- The only path from `run_agent` to cron was `tools.cronjob_tools`. It is now imported only when an agent's toolsets include the cronjob tool.

## Verification

- **Byte-identical output:** `get_tool_definitions()` for `hermes-cli`, `hermes-gateway`, `browser`, `web+terminal+file` and "all", plus `AIAgent.tools` and `build_system_prompt()` for three toolset selections, diffed byte-identical between the lazy path and `discover_builtin_tools()` run first.
- **`tests/tools/test_registry_lazy_discovery.py`:**
  - each lookup kind imports only what it needs;
  - opaque modules are never missed;
  - a shadowing registration meets the deferred built-in it would replace;
  - deregistering a deferred tool sticks;
  - the launch profile is bound during deferred imports;
  - a failed import is logged and not retried;
  - static-index cases are covered;
  - an E2E probe confirms the index equals what every built-in module actually registers.
- **`tests/perf_guards/test_run_agent_import_budget.py`:** a fresh interpreter against a temp `HERMES_HOME` checks two contracts and two ceilings.
  - Contracts: discovery stays deferred, and the import loads no `cron.*` module and no gateway runtime (`gateway.run`, `gateway.platforms.base`, `gateway.session`, `gateway.delivery`). Both fail on the parent commit.
  - Ceilings: best of 3 warm imports ≤ 3 s, and peak RSS ≤ 150 MB. These are coarse backstops against gross bloat, per the runner's ≥ 2 s wall-clock rule.
- **`scripts/run_tests.sh tests/tools/ tests/agent/ tests/perf_guards/`:** 22,897 passed. All 28 failures and 17 errors (14 files) reproduce identically on the parent commit on this machine. Causes:
  - fixtures whose `git commit` hits commit signing without the ssh-agent the runner strips;
  - no `keyring` in the test interpreter;
  - the macOS `/private/var` path alias;
  - host TTS, audio and bot-desktop backends.
- **Targeted cross-area run:** 436 passed (22 files across gateway platforms, plugins, doctor, banner, batch runner, cron and providers).
- `python scripts/check` is clean.

## Deliberately not changed

- **`tools.environments.local_env_policy`** builds its secret blocklist at import and pulls `gateway.config` / `config_env` / `platform_env` / `shutdown_watchdog` / `restart` (5 small modules, ~4 ms). `_build_adapter_secret_env` is documented to *fail the import* rather than drop secrets from the policy, so deferring it would move a fail-closed import error to a spawn-time miss.
- **`cron/__init__.py`** eagerly imports `cron.scheduler`, and the restart-safe worker runs as `-m cron.scheduler` through that package init. Making it lazy changes how the worker's `__main__` relates to `cron.scheduler`, so it needs its own PR.
- **`tools/cronjob_tools.py`** binds 13 `cron.jobs` names at module level, and 30 test files patch them there. Moving those imports into functions means moving every patch seam with them.
- **Plugin discovery** at `model_tools` import is now the largest remaining cost (~0.21–0.25 s warm). It loads ~110 plugin modules, plus `httpx`/`requests` via the bundled `dashboard_auth` and `browser_use` plugins. With no `config.yaml`, `load_config_readonly()` also runs uncached ~32×, once per plugin load deadline. Deferring plugin loads changes hook and provider registration timing, so it is a separate change.

prs.title: Gateway and serve no longer hoard free memory across ~160 malloc arenas
prs.body:
The gateway hands almost every new thread its own glibc memory pool and never gives those pools back, so a gateway that has been up for hours carries hundreds of MB of memory that is free but still counted against it. Now the gateway and `hermes serve` share at most 4 such pools, so freed memory gets reused instead of piling up, with no measurable speed cost.

**Outcome:** the long-lived Hermes server processes cap glibc malloc arenas at 4 (`runtime.malloc_arena_max`), shrinking free-but-held native memory without changing anything users can do.

## Why

glibc creates a new malloc arena for each thread that allocates while under its limit (8 x CPU cores) and keeps every arena's freed pages. A gateway starts ~1,100 short-lived Python threads per hour (tool heartbeats, turn watchdogs, stream monitors, pipe drains) on top of native pools (the relay plugin's tokio runtime, anydoc's rayon pool), so it fills every slot. Read-only `/proc` census of a 10-hour production gateway (20 cores, 191 threads, 2.0 GB RSS): **157 of the 160 possible 64 MiB arena heaps were mapped.**

## Change

- `hermes_cli/resource_limits.py::apply_malloc_arena_max` calls `mallopt(M_ARENA_MAX, n)` in-process, next to the existing `RLIMIT_NOFILE` floor in gateway bootstrap and `web_server.start_server` (serve / dashboard).
- New key `runtime.malloc_arena_max` (default `4`; `0`/`false`/`null` = glibc default), documented in `configuration.md` and `cli-config.yaml.example`.
- In-process rather than exporting `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` in the systemd unit / launchd plist / Desktop spawn env: one call covers every launch path (service, Desktop, detached auto-start, docker), and child commands (terminal tools, MCP servers, builds) keep glibc's default instead of inheriting a cap meant for the server.
- An operator's own `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` or `GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.arena_max` wins. macOS / Windows / musl: no-op.

## Measured (scratch `gateway run --force`, real Nous `gemini-3.8-flash` tool turns via api_server)

Host was heavily loaded by other work (loadavg 45-100 on 20 cores), so latency rows are noisy; RSS and arena counts are not.

| Workload | Leg | arena heaps (peak) | peak RSS | RSS after idle + trim | turn p50 / p90 | gateway CPU |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 concurrent x 4 tool turns | main, run 1 | 83 | 321 MB | 317 MB | 10.2 / 18.0 s | 10.8 s |
| | main, run 2 | 100 | 327 MB | 322 MB | 9.5 / 13.1 s | 9.8 s |
| | head (cap 4), run 1 | 6 | 322 MB | 314 MB | 14.9 / 37.0 s | 12.6 s |
| | head (cap 4), run 2 | 5 | 305 MB | 302 MB | 9.4 / 13.4 s | 10.6 s |
| | main + `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2` x2 | 0 / 0 | 300 / 304 MB | 295 / 298 MB | 12.9 / 11.4 s p50 | 10.6 / 10.9 s |

(The two head runs above also carried a separate timer-trim change; the heavier A/B below is this PR alone vs main.)

Heavier A/B, this PR alone vs main (12 concurrent x 5 turns with ~170 KB tool outputs; glibc `mallinfo2` sampled in-process every 5 s by a probe loaded into the scratch gateway; 10 of 60 turns in each leg hit the same provider connection errors):

| Leg | arena heaps | malloc arena bytes (peak) | of which free, held by malloc | peak RSS | RSS after idle + trim | gateway CPU (50 turns) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| main | 88 | 165 MB | **78 MB** | 349 MB | 343 MB | 23.7 s |
| head (cap 4) | 6 | 115 MB | **22 MB** (19 MB at end) | 344 MB | 339 MB | 28.0 s |
| main, run 2 (12 x 5 short tool turns) | 95 | 139 MB | **62 MB** | 329 MB | 325 MB | 16.3 s |
| head, run 2 (12 x 5 short tool turns) | 7 | 97 MB | **21 MB** | 315 MB | 307 MB | 16.4 s |

Read honestly: the cap removes ~75% of the free memory malloc keeps inside arenas and a third of the arena footprint, but RSS in a 6-minute scratch run moves only 5-22 MB, because the 60 s housekeeping `malloc_trim(0)` already hands most free arena pages back between bursts. The cap matters for what is resident between trims (the production gateway's log shows RSS regrowing 120-150 MB within each 60 s trim interval across its 157 arenas) and for every process where trims are off or cooled down; the scratch runs cannot reproduce 10 hours of uptime. Gateway CPU: run 1 +18% and run 2 +0.9% on a host at loadavg 40-80, i.e. inside that host's run-to-run spread; the microbenchmark below is the controlled measurement.

Allocator microbenchmark (16 threads of json + zlib + sha256 + sqlite, 7 interleaved runs each, same host):

| `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` | min wall | median wall | median RSS |
|---|---|---|---|
| glibc default | 4.45 s | 4.97 s | 53.6 MB |
| 4 | 3.95 s | 5.00 s | 49.7 MB |
| 2 | 4.23 s | 5.36 s | 47.0 MB |

Second run, CPU time (7 interleaved runs each): default median wall 3.14 s / CPU 5.24 s / RSS 53.5 MB; cap 4 median wall 3.16 s / CPU 5.44 s / RSS 44.6 MB. So in a worst-case stress where 16 threads allocate natively at the same time, the cap costs ~4% CPU from arena-lock waits and no wall time; a gateway's threads mostly hold or wait on the GIL, which already serialises their allocations.

4 is the default because it matches glibc's default on throughput while still collapsing ~100 arenas; 2 saves a little more memory but its median was the slowest.

## Tests

`tests/hermes_cli/test_malloc_arena_cap.py` (Linux): a child process that applies the cap and then runs 24 threads allocating at once maps <= 2 arena heaps, while the uncapped control maps >= 12; an operator `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` makes `apply_malloc_arena_max` a no-op. Red on main (no cap), green on head. `test_resource_limits.py`, `test_import_preserves_tui_cwd.py`, `test_multiplex_requires_default_profile.py` green (run from a tree copy under a fake HOME: the home-I/O guard trips on `.worktrees/` paths).

## Thread census (what the extra threads are; not changed here)

- 20 `tokio-rt-worker`: one tokio runtime per process, owned by the relay plugin's native extension (`nemo_relay/_native`, default workers = cores). Pooled, not leaked.
- 20 `Thread-2720 (_r…`: anydoc's rayon global pool, spawned once at the first document conversion. Linux threads inherit the creating thread's name, and the creator was an execute_code kernel's `_rpc_forever` thread (#2720). Pooled, not leaked.
- `Thread-NNNN (_…` triples: three reader/RPC threads per live execute_code kernel, bounded by `code_execution.max_session_kernels` and the 30-minute idle reaper.
None of these cost much on their own (idle thread stacks are a few KB of RSS); what they cost is one malloc arena each, which is what this PR caps.

![infographic](https://v3b.fal.media/files/b/0ab0ce9b/02TUKktnYquvaMDLLvs7Z_MyUHvv0j.png)

prs.title: fix(desktop): every gateway's sessions stay visible in Gateway & profile and Project grouping (salvage #141842, #146576)
prs.body:
## Summary

Desktop with several registered gateways and **All profiles** on: no row disappears or lands under the wrong gateway in **Gateway & profile** or **Project** grouping.

Salvages #141842 (@Bridgerz), cherry-picked with authorship kept. Builds on the idea in #146576 (@theenigmafield): the primary gateway's sessions go in one sidebar section. Credited with `Co-authored-by` plus their contributor-email commit. Their PR is not closed.

### Bugs (live on main, 3-gateway rig: This device default/research/writer, Homelab and Studio as real `hermes serve` remotes, 19 seeded sessions)

1. **Gateway & profile.** The primary's rows have no tag. Their profile groups showed as root groups with no header, mixed in among the remote gateway sections: `default` sat on top and `research` sat between Homelab and Studio. A `writer` group also appeared twice, once under This device and once as an empty "No sessions yet" root. With the window switched to Homelab, every local profile was filed **under Homelab** and the This device header was gone (#141842).
2. **Project.** The project tree comes from the window's gateway only. Rows owned by another gateway matched no project and vanished. Home said "Show all 7 sessions", and 12 remote chats appeared nowhere.

### Fix

- `e21be22` (@Bridgerz, #141842): Electron tags the primary aggregate's untagged rows with their real owner when the window is pinned to another gateway.
- `gateway-groups.tsx`: groups built from untagged rows keep their own unassigned id and render **inside the registry primary's section**. Routing already resolves those rows to the primary. Each profile appears once: the bare pool and rows tagged with the primary merge into a single group. Untagged groups are placed after tagged ones, so section order is unchanged.
- `projects/gateway-project-rows.ts` + `use-gateway-project-tree.ts`: rows owned by another gateway are filed the way that gateway files its own. Rows with no folder go under Home and are counted there. The rest go under a project for their folder on that gateway. A project name that two sources share gets ` · <gateway>` in its label.
- `main.ts` / `ChatSidebar` end at their `origin/main` size: two helpers moved into `profile-session-routing.ts`.

### Design note (why not #146576 verbatim)

#146576 reassigns untagged rows to the primary inside `buildGatewaySessionGroups`. That turns 3 `origin/main` assertions red in `gateway-group-model.test.ts` and `gateway-groups.test.tsx` (bbba4d4f772: "leaves legacy rows without a connection unassigned", and the `[null, 'default']` totals group). It also fails 4 cases in `gateway-groups-webapp.test.tsx` (927fe54ff18: empty profile sections stay with the untagged pool). This PR gets the same visible result at render time, so every main test passes unchanged.

### Live A/B (native Electron on Xvfb; `origin/main` 557254faa24 vs this branch; All profiles on)

Rows per group out of 19 seeded:

| View | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| Gateway & profile, window on This device | default 3 and research 2 as headerless roots; This device › writer 2; duplicate empty `writer` root | Homelab 7 (3/2/2) · Studio 5 (3/2) · **This device 7 (writer 2, default 3, research 2)**; no roots, no duplicates |
| Gateway & profile, window on Homelab | local default/research/writer **under Homelab**; no This device header | Homelab 7 · Studio 5 · This device 7 |
| Project, window on This device | Home "Show all 7"; 12 remote rows nowhere | Home 11 (7 local + 4 folder-less remote) · app · Studio 3 · app · Homelab 2 · infra 3 = 19 |
| Project, window on Homelab | Home "Show all 7" | Home 16 · app 3 = 19 |

Screenshots (main = base leg, this PR = head leg; every shot was vision-checked, with no error cards):

| | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| Gateway & profile | ![](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/teknium1/126ef6ebfc780804fc729e08efa07912/raw/base-Gatewayprofile.png) | ![](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/teknium1/126ef6ebfc780804fc729e08efa07912/raw/head-Gatewayprofile.png) |
| Gateway & profile, on Homelab | ![](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/teknium1/126ef6ebfc780804fc729e08efa07912/raw/base-homelab-Gatewayprofile.png) | ![](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/teknium1/126ef6ebfc780804fc729e08efa07912/raw/head-homelab-Gatewayprofile.png) |
| Project | ![](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/teknium1/126ef6ebfc780804fc729e08efa07912/raw/base-Project.png) | ![](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/teknium1/126ef6ebfc780804fc729e08efa07912/raw/head-Project.png) |
| Project, on Homelab | ![](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/teknium1/126ef6ebfc780804fc729e08efa07912/raw/base-homelab-Project.png) | ![](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/teknium1/126ef6ebfc780804fc729e08efa07912/raw/head-homelab-Project.png) |

### Tests

- `gateway-groups-primary-pool.test.tsx`: fails on `origin/main` (checked). It asserts that untagged primary rows plus a primary profile tagged twice end up in one This device section, with one group per profile.
- `projects/gateway-project-rows.test.ts`: every row from another gateway lands in exactly one project, folder-less rows are counted in Home, and same-name projects get the gateway in their label.
- `vitest run src/app/chat/sidebar electron/profile-session-routing.test.ts electron/main`: 54 files, 472 tests, all passing. `tsc --noEmit` passes. `scripts/check --only health` passes.

### Not covered / decisions

- **This device first.** The mockup puts This device first. Main's `gateway-groups-drag.test.tsx` pins the default section order (insertion/recency) without a hand-picked order, so this PR keeps that order. Putting the primary first is a separate decision.
- Project actions on a project that exists only on another gateway (new session in it, dismiss) still act on the window's gateway.

prs.title: Old phone-app chats continue in Desktop instead of opening read-only
prs.body:
Phone apps that signed in through the dashboard login used to save their chats under their own label (`mobile`, `ios`). On current main, Desktop opens those old chats but won't let you keep typing. Now they continue like any Desktop chat. Chats written by a separate WebUI process, messaging-platform rows, and old cron, subagent or curator runs stay read-only. The hermes-mobile plugin's own chats are not affected.

Old phone-app chats labelled with the app's own name can be continued from native Desktop, the TUI and `hermes sessions adopt`.

## What changes

Live run: a real gateway daemon in a scratch home, reached over the native connection Desktop and `hermes sessions adopt` use (`connect_gateway`). The model points at a dead loopback port, so no provider was called. Each row is `session.resume` followed by `prompt.submit`:

| stored row | main e8639fd4312 | this PR (7b9300ae1cc) |
|---|---|---|
| `source='mobile'`, no stamp | opens, prompt refused: `session_read_only` | opens, prompt accepted |
| `source='ios'`, `user_id='basic:admin'` | opens, prompt refused: `session_read_only` | opens, prompt accepted |
| `source='desktop'`, `basic:admin` (control, #145598) | opens, prompt accepted | opens, prompt accepted |
| `source='webui'` (third-party WebUI writer) | read-only | read-only |
| `source='cron'`, `'curator'` | read-only | read-only |
| `source='teams'` (bundled platform plugin) | read-only | read-only |

After the gateway restarts (fresh daemon, fresh client), both phone chats reopen with their history and accept a prompt. State readback after adoption: `source=desktop`, `created_source=mobile` / `ios` (provenance kept), owner `uid:1000`, local route bound.

A routed `source='mobile'` row from the hermes-mobile plugin (`Platform('mobile')`) still resumes on its messaging route. The closed community PRs #147243 and #147286 turned that case into `not_found`.

## How

- `hermes_state_local_migration.py`: a new `client_label(source)` accepts any label that is not:
  - a local surface;
  - a shipped messaging platform (the enum plus bundled platform plugins);
  - an automation, recovery or foreign-writer label (`cron, subagent, kanban, bot_room, a2a, webhook, api_server, import, recovered, curator, batch, homeassistant, webui, local, unknown`).

  `client_history_row` is a client label on a row with no route. Adoption resumes these rows as `gui`. Binding relabels them `desktop`: once bound the row has a route, and its old label would then read as a messaging chat.
- `gateway/session_local_migration.py::adopts_client_history`: resume adopts such a row only when all three hold:
  - the native owner asks (Desktop, TUI or CLI, the same gate legacy adoption uses);
  - the row validates for that owner (`validate_legacy_row`: same profile, owner stamp or none);
  - the session isn't already open on this gateway.

  Anyone else still gets the read-only history mount.
- The same predicate is used for:
  - sidebar edits (`hermes_state_mutation_binding.py`);
  - the stored picker (`gateway/session_listing.py`);
  - `hermes sessions adopt` (SQL pre-filter, so cron/subagent bulk never gets resolved row by row);
  - `/handoff` reopen (`handed_off_ref` accepts an adopted chat's `created_source`).
- Docs: the adoption paragraph in `website/docs/user-guide/desktop.md`.

Root cause: the pre-authority `hermes serve` stored whatever `source` a client sent, and adoption only knew the local surfaces' own labels.

## Tests

`tests/gateway/test_legacy_client_label_adoption.py` (real session authority):
- `mobile` and stamped `ios` rows resume writable and stay resumable. `webui`, `teams` and `curator` rows stay read-only. Red on main: `session_read_only`.
- A plugin platform's routed `mobile` row keeps its messaging route. This is the control: green on main and on head.

Local regression run: every test file that references the touched symbols (270 files outside e2e), 3446 passed, 0 failed. `test_hermes_state.py` hit the local 300 s per-file cap under load; CI runs it.

## Review

An independent reviewer worked through the PR. Two rounds found no P1/P2. Boundaries probed:
- another profile's row: `not_found`;
- a foreign owner stamp: stays read-only;
- non-native callers: refused, same as main;
- the plugin `mobile` route: unchanged.

P3 folds in b057b11b2a0, plus one bot finding in 7b9300ae1cc (`hermes sessions adopt` skipped login-stamped phone chats; now judged for the host owner):
- Bundled platform plugins and the curator/batch labels were adoptable.
- `hermes sessions adopt` was about 7× slower on an 18k-session store (0.9 s → 6.6 s); it now pre-filters.
- An adopted phone chat lost the `/handoff` reopen.

Not changed: a read-only history mount that another reader opened earlier in the same gateway process keeps the owner on read-only until it is evicted. That is no worse than main, and swapping a live mount out from under its viewers is a separate change.

Refs #146814, #144814, #143547 (RT-30b).

prs.title: fix(desktop): publish the request connection and its profile together
prs.body:
## What

Desktop never sends a request for a (gateway, profile) pair that does not exist while switching. The ambient REST request connection and the profile it serves are now published in one notification frame, and the shared-metrics consent read takes both halves from that scope.

## Why

On a switch from a local profile to an SSH gateway (alpha on This device -> default on Box), `applyActive` in `store/gateway.ts` published the request connection before the profile mirror (`store/profile.ts`) moved the profile. For one synchronous step `$apiRequestScope` was (box, alpha). The version poller (`store/updates.ts`) listens to that atom and fired in the gap, so main dialed a remote backend for profile alpha on Box: a stray per-profile `hermes serve` plus an SSH control master, and `Error: Profile 'alpha' does not exist` in its remote log. This bug was already on main.

A second channel did the same thing on the way back (Box -> alpha). `useDesktopMetrics` paired `$activeConnectionId` (the connection descriptor, published only after the activation settles) with the active gateway profile (moved inside `applyActive`), so `shared_metrics.status` went out as `requestGatewayForAgent(box, alpha)`.

## How

- `store/gateway-request-scope.ts` `publishRequestConnection(connectionId, profile)`: inside one nanostores `batch`, when the connection moves, the profile half is set to the profile the route serves on that connection, and then the connection is set. Every writer of the connection half goes through it (`applyActive`, `setPrimaryGateway`, `setPrimaryGatewayConnectionId`). On the same connection the profile half is left to the profile mirror, because a shared-primary socket serves profiles other than its own route's.
- `useDesktopMetrics` reads connection and profile from `$apiRequestScope` together.
- `applyActive` publishes the socket, gateway state, request scope and route profile in ONE `batch`. Before, `$gateway` listeners ran before the profile was published. The display-toggle connect push, for one, paired the new socket's connection with the old route's profile.
- Settings re-home and cold boot (`use-gateway-boot.ts`) look up the primary's profile on the new machine BEFORE recording the connection. They publish `(connection, profile)` through `setPrimaryGatewayConnection(conn, profile)` → `publishRequestConnection`. `adoptPrimaryProfile` reuses that lookup.

## Tests

- `src/store/gateway-request-scope-pair.test.ts` uses the real registry and the real request scope and listens to every scope emission. On main it fails with `['box|alpha', 'box|default']` for the switch and `box|alpha` for a primary re-home. On this branch it passes. A third case is a control: a same-connection re-publish keeps the mirror's profile.
- Full `vitest run src`: 1499 files / 12636 tests pass. `tsc -p .` is clean. `scripts/check --only health` is ok.

## Review round (74e909d65f5)
- **Settings soft re-home still published new gateway/old profile (3cae7d4b713).** `softSwitch` recorded Box's connection while the primary profile was still local's alpha. It then awaited the ticket mint and connect before adopting Box's profile. During that wait the scope read `box|alpha`, and the version poller called `getVersion({connectionId:'box', profile:'alpha'})`. Fixed as described above; boot had the same shape and is fixed too. New `use-gateway-boot-rehome-scope.test.tsx` drives the real hook: boot local/alpha, start the real update poller, apply a Settings switch to box/default, and hold the ticket mint. The scope is `box|default` mid-switch, `box|alpha` is never emitted, and `getVersion` is never called for box/alpha. It is red on 520684bb7ff. The PR's own pair test reversed the production call order; it now records the connection (with its profile) before adopting the socket.
- **`$gateway` listeners saw a half-published route (4decc8e4664).** Found in #147797's review (display auto-push). New pair-test case: a `$gateway` listener on a switch to box/gamma reads `box|gamma|gamma`. It was `box|alpha|alpha` on 520684bb7ff.
- **74e909d65f5** moves `RegistryConfig`, unchanged, into `store/gateway-registry-config.ts`, so `store/gateway.ts` stays under its line ratchet.
- Merged with #147797's head: `git merge-tree` is clean, and the new tests from both PRs pass together (7/7).

## Live A/B

The rig: real native Electron (Xvfb) and real `hermes serve` backends. A local alpha primary, an SSH gateway Box behind a private sshd (profiles default/gamma/delta), and a URL remote Lan (default/eps). Each leg ran 3 rounds of rail clicks: alpha -> Box default -> alpha.

| leg | `conn:box::alpha` routes | stray remote spawns after the switches start | `Profile 'alpha' does not exist` |
|---|---|---|---|
| main 557254f | 1 | 1 (17:48:18, right after alpha -> Box) | 1 |
| head, first commit only | 1 (Box -> alpha, the metrics read; stack traced to `shared_metrics.status`) | 1 | 1 |
| head 520684b | 0 | 0 | 0 |

Control on head: local default <-> alpha and Lan eps <-> local alpha routes land on their own pairs (`conn:local::default`, `alpha`, `conn:lan::eps`), with no mixed route and no stray spawn.

## Not covered

Other consumers still pair `$activeConnectionId` with `$activeGatewayProfile`. The two atoms move at different times during a switch: the profile moves in `applyActive`, and the descriptor moves in the later publication batch. None of these consumers dialed a stray in the rig.

## Infographic

![pair-race](https://v3b.fal.media/files/b/0ab0ca9f/FScpogrPLL1pnCNtkfWdR_x282gUtJ.png)
