prs.title: feat(gateway): opt-in OIDC dashboard sign-in
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - Adds opt-in dashboard sign-in through a configured `[oidc.<alias>]` provider. Until now the dashboard could only be unlocked with a pairing code, so every paired browser was the shared operator, even though the CLI, zerocode and RPC already sign in with OIDC.
  - **New `[gateway.dashboard_sign_in]` table**, empty by default. With it absent nothing changes: no new screen, no cookie is read, and every existing route behaves as before. Turning it on requires `gateway.require_pairing = true`. The config error names the fix, including for the Docker image's default config.
  - **The browser flow reuses the existing relay:** Authorization Code + PKCE on the existing flow store, limits and `/oidc/callback` redirect URI.
    - The flow is bound to the browser that started it by a per-flow cookie.
    - The ID token is required as evidence of the sign-in (a new `Enrollment::pkce_exchange_requiring_id_token`), then discarded.
    - The access token is verified by the configured provider exactly as RPC verifies a bearer. Service principals and identities with no mapped profile are refused.
    - The token only ever goes to the provider it was issued by. The callback takes the provider's issuer and client and its code-exchange client from one reading of the configuration. Sign-in and every later re-verification then check that issuer and client against the same accepted policy that would send the token (a new `RpcInboundAuth::authenticate_bound` in the runtime). A provider repointed meanwhile gets nothing.
  - **The gateway keeps the token in memory** behind an opaque `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Strict` session cookie (`__Host-` and `Secure` over HTTPS at the root). Every request carrying the cookie is checked again against the same inbound authority RPC uses: expiry, the introspection deadline, and grants at the current policy generation.
  - **CSRF:** requests that change state need the session's `X-ZeroClaw-CSRF` token, and cookie-carrying requests and WebSocket upgrades must come from the dashboard's own origin. An `Authorization` header always wins over the cookie.
  - **What a signed-in account reaches:**
    - administrators (a profile with `admin = true`) reach every page, as a paired browser does;
    - other accounts reach the config pages their grants allow, and get 403 `operator_required` elsewhere.
  - **Re-verification across a policy change:** a re-verification that a policy publish lands in the middle of is tried once more with the same token and the same provider, as the grants check already is. A compatible change then keeps the session.
  - **Expiry, sign-out and sockets:** an expiring session shows a re-auth prompt in a popup that keeps the page. Sign-out is local and spans tabs. The chat socket, event stream, canvas and SOP-run feeds close at once when their session ends or loses access. That includes a running chat turn, which finishes unattended with any pending tool approval refused. They also close when the gateway reloads, so the new configuration decides on reconnect. The canvas and SOP-run feeds close on both even while their first frames are still going to a client that has stopped reading. A check that has to verify the session again with the identity provider cannot admit anything after the session's hard expiry or the reload; a request that reaches the gateway being replaced, over a connection that stayed open, gets `503` and is retried. Signing in again in a browser ends the session it held before, whoever's it was, so a later sign-out leaves nothing of that browser signed in. That holds when two sign-ins in one browser overlap too, in whatever order their steps arrive: browser marker cookies tie the browser's sessions together, the sign-in that finishes later ends the other, and sign-out ends every session that shares a marker with the browser. A config write or operator request admitted before its session ended is refused where it acts: under the config write lock, or where the route decides after reading its body.
  - **Web:** the sign-in screen with provider buttons above the unchanged pairing form, session state, the CSRF header, 401/403 reason routing, one close rule for every signed-in socket (chat, Runs, Canvas and the event stream), the account menu, navigation by access, and strings for every locale. Desktop keeps pairing.
    - The close rule: no timed reconnect on 4401/4403 or while a re-auth is pending, one reconnect after re-authentication, and a normal reconnect on 1001.
    - A 4401 first re-checks the session, so an early re-authentication moves the socket to the new session without another prompt.
    - A 401 `session_invalid` re-checks it too before signing out. A request sent under a session the browser has since replaced keeps the page, and a read is sent again on the new session.
    - A chat turn whose socket closed mid-turn ends locally, and the transcript reloads when the socket reopens.
- **Scope boundary:**
  - No refresh tokens: the user signs in again on expiry.
  - No single sign-out at the identity provider.
  - Sign-out within one browser has two limits. A sign-in already at the identity provider when the browser signs out still finishes and starts a new session. A browser that refuses the marker cookie keeps the earlier behaviour: signing in again still ends the session it held, but of two sign-ins that overlap, the first one's session can outlive sign-out until it expires.
  - No password login (#8076), SCIM or SAML.
  - No change to pairing, the CLI, zerocode or RPC.
  - Chat for non-administrator accounts through the core's session methods is a follow-up.
  - The chat socket's sends outside a streamed turn (`session_start`, error replies, pongs and a turn's terminal frames) don't yet give way to a session that ends while one of them is stalled. That is #12125.
  - Nothing for the separate `zeroclaw-gw` process.
- **Blast radius:**
  - **Gateway auth on every route.** A router-wide layer classifies cookie-carrying requests, and `require_auth`, the config route layer and the inline pairing checks (event stream, chat, canvas, SOP runs, plugin list) admit a session. With sign-in off, the layer never reads a cookie.
  - **Config:** `zeroclaw-config` gains one additive table.
  - **Runtime:** `zeroclaw-runtime` gains one exchange variant and `RpcInboundAuth::authenticate_bound`. Their placement exceptions are recorded in #11963, now merged. Plain `authenticate` is unchanged.
  - **Gateway serving:** the native TLS listener now serves HTTP/1 upgrades, as the plain listener does, so the dashboard's sockets work over `[gateway.tls]`. Before, they were dropped right after their `101` (#11951). This is one self-contained commit, which can also ship on its own.
  - **Web:** `web/src/lib/{auth,api,ws,sse}.ts` and `hooks/useAuth.ts`, which every page goes through. In pairing mode their behaviour is unchanged.
- **Linked issue(s):**
  - Closes #11961
  - Closes #11951
  - Part of #8289
  - Related #7432
  - Builds on #11963, merged: the placement rows for this PR's two runtime additions, with the Core approval recorded in each row
  - Builds on #11901 and #11903, both merged. This branch carried their commits until they landed; since the master merge `b0ed40c2b1` they are in its base and no longer in this PR's diff
  - Follow-up #12125 (the chat socket's other sends, found in review)

### What this does, simply

A team that already signs in to ZeroClaw's CLI with its identity provider still had to hand out pairing codes for the web dashboard, and anyone with a code got full access. With this change an operator can add one table to the config and the dashboard offers "Sign in with <provider>".

The browser never holds the token: the gateway keeps it and gives the browser a cookie that script cannot read. Each request is checked against the same rules the CLI and RPC already follow. Administrators get the whole dashboard. Other accounts get only what their profile allows, which in this change is the configuration their profile grants.

When a sign-in expires the page stays as it was and asks the user to sign in again in a small window. Signing out of ZeroClaw doesn't sign the user out of the identity provider. Installs that don't add the table see no difference at all.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes, once CI is green.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `web` (dashboard), through the gateway.
- **Setup / preconditions:**
  - An OIDC provider (Keycloak works) with a client that uses Authorization Code + PKCE (S256).
  - The client's redirect URI is `<dashboard origin>/oidc/callback`, its access tokens carry the configured `audience` (RFC 9068 `at+jwt` for JWKS validation), and it has a groups claim.
  - The config: `[gateway] require_pairing = true`; `[gateway.dashboard_sign_in] oidc = ["corp"]`; and `[oidc.corp]` with `interactive_clients = ["<client id>"]` and a `profile_map` with one group mapped to an `admin = true` profile and one to a profile granting `config = ["read"]`.
  - Serve over HTTPS, or open the dashboard on `localhost`.
- **Steps to run:**
  1. Open the dashboard and choose "Sign in with corp". Sign in as an administrator.
  2. Open a few pages.
  3. Sign out in one tab while another tab is open.
  4. Sign in as the other account; open a non-config page by URL.
  5. Set the client's token lifespan to 60 s and wait.
  6. Remove the table and reload.
- **Expected on this branch (after):**
  1. You land on the dashboard with no token in local or session storage, and `document.cookie` doesn't show the session.
  2. Every page loads.
  3. Both tabs show the signed-out screen.
  4. "Not available for your account".
  5. A re-auth prompt keeps the page; the same account resumes.
  6. The pairing dialog is back, and the old cookie no longer works.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** only the pairing dialog. There is no way to sign in with the provider, and the callback page shows a token to copy.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:**
  - Rust format, clippy (`-D warnings`) and tests for `zeroclaw-config`, `zeroclaw-runtime` and `zeroclaw-gateway`, which cover:
    - the config validation (four tests);
    - the required-ID-token exchange (two);
    - the token's provider binding: a sign-in callback with publications landing between its steps and during a delayed exchange, a sign-in whose pin no longer matches, and a re-verification whose provider is repointed to another issuer or client mid-verification. Each must send the token to no other provider. A compatible publish keeps the session;
    - the runtime's `authenticate_bound` (another issuer, another client, no such provider);
    - a signed-in socket over native TLS closing `1001` when the gateway stops, and an upgrade racing the stop over TLS;
    - the gateway sign-in flow against a mock provider (start, binding, callback, session, sign-out), origin and CSRF refusals, bearer precedence, refusals of service and unmapped identities, HTTPS-or-loopback, the return-path guard, the store caps, expiry, a removed or repointed provider, a policy change, re-verification after a reload, turning sign-in off, and socket watches. It also covers real chat sockets that close on sign-out, expiry or a lost admin grant, both mid-turn and between turns, including a message waiting for the session's turn; an approval sent after sign-out that resolves nothing; a canvas feed that does not outlive a reload; canvas and SOP-run feeds whose first frames stall on a client that has stopped reading, which still release their session watch on sign-out and on reload; signing in again in one browser, which ends the session it held (also when only the callback carries its cookie, never on a refused sign-in, and whichever account held it); two sign-ins that overlap in one browser, where the later ends the earlier and sign-out ends both, in every order of their starts, start answers and callbacks (a start answered only after the other sign-in finished among them), also with a refused sign-in and an ended session's cookie, while another browser stays signed in; a browser marker that authorizes nothing; a config write and an operator request whose session ends while their body is still arriving, both refused; the zeroizing token store; and the idle sweep of expired sessions.
  - The architecture tests.
  - The docs gates for the authentication guide and the ADR-017 text.
  - `Web Permission Tests` (`cargo web check`, `tsc -b`, the existing web suites and the new `npm run test:auth`), which cover:
    - the startup decision;
    - CSRF and no-bearer headers;
    - 401/403 routing;
    - socket close codes, including the Runs page itself and a socket closed mid-turn;
    - a request or stream refused under a session the browser has since replaced, which keeps the page;
    - navigation access;
    - the sign-in screen ("sign-in off renders the old pairing dialog");
    - expiry and re-auth;
    - cross-tab sign-out;
    - every locale carrying the new strings.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:**
  - No run against a real identity provider in CI.
  - The revert-the-fix checks below are not CI jobs.
- **CI on `02314854b3`:** every check passes, `Semgrep OSS` included. On `34bfd2d475` (tidux's master merge) only `Semgrep OSS` (report-only) failed, on the `ws://` request in the stalled-feed test, which reaches only that test's own loopback listener; the `nosemgrep` marker added in `ae66999dee`, like the existing one in the same file, covers it.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- **New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope?** Yes.
  - An account whose permission profile has `admin = true` can now use the whole dashboard after signing in, as a paired browser can.
  - Other accounts get only the config routes their grants allow; everything else answers 403.
  - Each sign-in is logged with the principal it resolved to.
- **New external network calls?** Yes, to the configured provider only:
  - the code exchange, which the existing relay already makes;
  - the provider's JWKS or introspection endpoint when a session is verified again (at the introspection deadline, after a reload, or after a policy change).
  - A token is only ever sent to the issuer and client it was issued by, checked against the policy that would send it. A sign-in or session whose provider was repointed to another issuer or client is refused or ended without its token being sent anywhere.
- **Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed?** Yes.
  - The access token is kept in gateway memory for the session's life, in a buffer that is wiped when the session ends: on sign-out, expiry (expired sessions are swept every minute even when no request arrives), revocation, or when sign-in is turned off. It is never logged or written to disk. A refresh token the provider returns anyway is wiped unused.
  - The browser holds only an opaque `HttpOnly` session cookie and a CSRF token in memory, plus the browser marker below. A session cookie whose session ended is left in place, so every tab keeps hearing `session_expired`: it names nothing and holds no token. Sign-out clears it, also once the session has ended, and a new sign-in replaces it. The ID token is checked, then discarded. Its subject is not compared with the access token's principal: both come from the same back-channel exchange, and the account is the one the access token resolves to.
  - A sign-in's start gives a browser without one a marker cookie under a name of its own (`zc_browser_<tag>`, or `__Host-zc_browser_<tag>` over HTTPS at the root): random, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax` so that the provider's redirect carries it, with no expiry set. It names a browser, not an account, and authorizes nothing: the gateway reads at most eight per request, only at the callback, to tie the new session to the browser, and at sign-out.
  - Refresh tokens are neither relayed nor kept.
- **PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs?** No. The account display name comes from the verified token's claims and is shown only to that user.
- **Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed?** No.
- **Mitigations:**
  - login-CSRF binding per flow;
  - origin and CSRF checks, including WebSocket upgrades;
  - `__Host-` cookies where the deployment allows;
  - HTTPS required except on the gateway's own machine;
  - no CORS grants on cookie responses (asserted in tests);
  - session store caps that never evict another account (256 total, 8 per account; at the cap a sign-in is refused).
- **Documented limits ("Things to know" in the authentication guide):**
  - removing an administrator at the identity provider does not revoke devices they paired;
  - loopback HTTP cookies are port-agnostic;
  - an unreachable introspection endpoint ends a session that is due for revalidation (fails closed).

## Compatibility (required)

- **Backward compatible?** Yes.
- **Config / env / CLI surface changed?** Yes: the optional `[gateway.dashboard_sign_in]` table (`oidc`, `session_lifetime_secs`).
- **Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed?** No.
- **Upgrade steps for existing users:** none; it is off unless configured. To turn it on, see "Dashboard sign-in" in `docs/book/src/security/authentication.md`. Behind a reverse proxy, the browser's `Host` must reach the gateway unchanged.
- **From #11903, now merged:** with an OIDC entry that validates by JWKS (the default), a signed-in session could need a fresh sign-in after a reload.
  - Each reload starts with an empty key cache. While its first key fetch was in flight, the provider refused other verifications as misconfigured, and a browser's reconnects arrive together, so one of them could end the session.
  - #11903 makes concurrent checks share one fetch. It is on master and in this branch's base, and this PR changes nothing in that code. A re-verification that still fails logs `dashboard session ended: verifying its token again failed`.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** remove `[gateway.dashboard_sign_in]` (or empty `oidc`). Every session ends at its next request, or within a minute if none arrives, and the dashboard falls back to pairing. Then `git revert <sha>` if needed.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** `gateway.dashboard_sign_in.oidc`; empty means off.
- **Observable failure symptoms:**
  - gateway log events `dashboard sign-in` / `dashboard sign-in refused` / `dashboard sign-out`;
  - 401 bodies with `reason` `session_expired` / `session_invalid`, 403 with `csrf` / `origin` / `operator_required`, and, during a reload, 503 with `gateway_restarting`;
  - a pairing-only install showing anything other than the pairing dialog;
  - dashboard requests from a signed-in browser carrying `Authorization`.

## ADR note

ADR-017 (`proposed`) gains the dashboard session model under its token-purpose decision: a dashboard session is the browser's connection, and its token is kept in gateway memory as that session's revalidation context. Its OIDC acceptance gate now names dashboard sign-in, sign-out and re-authentication.

milestone.title: v0.9.0
milestone.description:
v0.9.0 prioritizes opt-in OIDC dashboard sign-in, principal isolation, schema V4 and a CLI-only build option.

The standard build keeps the working in-process dashboard. Sign-in stays off by default, preserving the existing pairing flow. Release gates are real-provider sign-in evidence; the five principal-isolation repairs (#11234, #11220, #11225, #11230, #11266, with #11198 tracked); schema V4 (#11218); and a build-time CLI-only option that omits gateway/web assets and directs dashboard users to the standard build.

Scoped dashboard chat has a November 3 go/no-go, with sign-in alone as the fallback. November 10 is the earliest target, subject to the gates, not a committed date.

Standalone zeroclaw-gw, full gateway IPC route/parity work, cross-process webhook handling and two-process desktop packaging move to v0.9.x. Channel listeners remain in core under existing documented exceptions. These deferrals do not complete the remaining gateway roadmap.

prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions)
- **What changed and why:**
  - Lifecycle-directory refusals print a pasteable `rm` / `chmod 700` / `sudo chown -R …` fix.
  - A relative config/data path whose first component starts with `-` (for example `ZEROCLAW_CONFIG_DIR=-install`) made those commands look like options to `rm` and GNU `chmod`/`chown`.
  - Prefix only those relative paths with `./` before shell-escaping, so the pasted command treats them as paths on Linux and macOS (BSD `chmod`/`chown` reject `--`).

prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions)
- **What changed and why:** The `native_tools` config doc comment claimed the field is "consulted only by the Groq factory". That is wrong: three provider factories consult it (`groq`, `custom`, `hailo_ollama`), and the `custom` (generic OpenAI-compatible) factory disables native tool calling unless `native_tools = true`. The comment now lists the consulting families and their defaults, the `tool_dispatcher` runtime-profile field documents what `"auto"` / `"native"` / `"xml"` actually select, and the Custom Providers page gains a short "Native tool calling" section with a TOML example.
- **Scope boundary:** Documentation only. No code, config parsing, or runtime behavior changes. The reworded comments flow into the generated config reference (`docs/book/src/reference/config.md`, gitignored) and rustdoc on the next generation run; no committed generated artifact changes.
- **Blast radius:** Anyone reading the config schema, the generated config reference, the Custom Providers page, or the Provider Configuration field list. No runtime consumer reads these comments.
- **Linked issue(s):** None.

### What this does, simply

An operator pointing ZeroClaw at a self-hosted OpenAI-compatible gateway via the `custom` provider slot may find that the agent never uses real tool calls. The gateway supports the OpenAI `tools` protocol, but ZeroClaw sends the tools as text in the system prompt and expects the model to answer with `<tool_call>` XML. Nothing in the `custom` slot docs said native tool calling is off by default, so the only clue was a schema comment that pointed at Groq. This PR corrects that comment to name the families that actually consult `native_tools` and their defaults, documents the `tool_dispatcher` strategies (including what happens if you force `"native"` on a provider that was built without native tool calling), and adds a "Native tool calling" section to the Custom Providers page with a `native_tools = true` example. prs.title: fix(providers): fail fast on quota-exhausted 429 error types
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - `is_non_retryable_rate_limit` now recognizes the `FreeUsageLimitError` (OpenCode Zen/Go) and `usage_limit_reached` error types as business 429s. OpenCode's quota-exhausted body says "Rate limit exceeded. Please try again later.", so the existing phrase list missed it. Each call then became 3 requests with 500 ms / 1 s backoff against a quota that cannot recover that fast.
  - The error type string is the signal. Generic wording such as "rate limit exceeded" is deliberately not matched, so ordinary transient 429s keep retrying.
  - All four non-streaming retry arms and `is_terminal_provider_failure` already route through this classifier, so they pick up the fail-fast behavior with no control-flow change.
- **Scope boundary:** This does not honor the HTTP `Retry-After` response header, which #10779 also asks for. Provider errors are plain text today, so that needs transport plumbing through `api_error` and the providers that build their own errors. As the triage suggested, that part is split into #11768. User-facing terminal text is unchanged: the existing `cli-agent-error-provider-rate-limited` message already says "review quota, or choose another provider".
- **Blast radius:** Retry and failover decisions in `ReliableModelProvider` for 429 responses whose body contains one of the two new type strings. Those now take the existing `rate_limited_non_retryable` path: one attempt, then the next candidate.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #10779 (classifier slice). The Retry-After header part is tracked in #11768.

### What this does, simply

When a provider says "your free quota is used up", ZeroClaw should stop and move to the next model or provider right away. Retrying a second later cannot help. OpenCode labels that case `FreeUsageLimitError` but words it like an ordinary "rate limit exceeded, try again later", so ZeroClaw kept retrying. ZeroClaw now reads the error type and fails fast. Real temporary rate limits still retry as before.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A. The behavior boundary is covered by a mock-provider test that counts physical attempts, and reproducing it live needs an exhausted OpenCode free quota.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** `cargo test` (providers unit tests), `Format`, and `Lint` on Linux cover the changed file.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** None.
- **Commands run and tail output:** Run locally on Windows with Rust 1.98.0, the CI-pinned toolchain.

```text
$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-providers --lib reliable::tests::non_retryable_rate_limit   # before the fix
test reliable::tests::non_retryable_rate_limit_detects_usage_limit_reached ... FAILED
test reliable::tests::non_retryable_rate_limit_detects_opencode_free_usage_limit ... FAILED
test reliable::tests::non_retryable_rate_limit_skips_retries_for_opencode_free_usage_limit ... FAILED
test result: FAILED. 5 passed; 3 failed

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-providers --lib reliable   # after the fix
test result: ok. 207 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 1740 filtered out

$ cargo fmt -p zeroclaw-providers   # no changes
$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-providers --all-targets   # no warnings in zeroclaw-providers
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?**
  - The new end-to-end test uses the exact error string from the issue's runtime trace. It asserts one physical attempt under `max_retries = 2` and a `rate_limited_non_retryable` failure reason.
  - A guard test pins that a non-429 error carrying `FreeUsageLimitError` is not flagged.

prs.title: fix(channels/email): mark live mail seen in active mode
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - In active mode (`observer_mode = false`) the startup drain fetches UNSEEN mail with `RFC822`, which sets `\Seen`. Mail that arrives while the session runs goes through `fetch_new`, which used `BODY.PEEK[]` in both modes, so it stayed unseen. The only other guard is the in-memory `seen_messages` set, which is empty after a restart, so the next startup drain handed every such email to the agent again and the sender got a second reply.
  - `fetch_new` now picks its FETCH item with `new_mail_fetch_item(observer_mode)`: `RFC822` in active mode, the same item and the same flag effect as the startup drain, and `BODY.PEEK[]` in observer mode.
  - Because the flag is set by the fetch, it also covers mail the channel fetches but does not hand to the agent (a sender outside the allowlist), which is no longer re-read and re-logged as blocked on every restart. That matches what the startup drain already does for the same mail.
- **Scope boundary:** observer mode is unchanged and still never changes a flag; it is not affected by the restart duplicate because every session starts from `UIDNEXT`. No persisted state, no config change, no change to the IDLE or polling loops (the delayed-mail issue in those loops is #11761, fixed separately).
- **Blast radius:** active-mode email channels. Mail delivered while the daemon runs now shows as read in other mail clients, as mail drained at startup already did.
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #11760

### What this does, simply

The email channel has two ways of reading mail: when it starts it reads everything unread, and while it runs it reads each new email as it arrives. The first way marks the email as read; the second did not. So every email that came in while the agent was running stayed "unread" on the server, and the next time the agent restarted it read those emails again and answered them a second time. Now, unless the channel is in observer mode (which promises never to touch the mailbox), new emails are marked read when they are fetched, exactly like the startup read does.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `channel` = `email`
- **Setup / preconditions:** an email channel with `observer_mode = false` on an IMAP server with IDLE (GreenMail or Dovecot work), the sender in the channel's peer group.
- **Steps to run:** start the daemon, send one email, wait for the reply, restart the daemon.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** the email shows `\Seen` on the server after the first reply; no second reply after the restart.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** the email is still unseen after the first reply, and the agent answers it again after the restart (same message id dispatched twice).

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** the required `Test` job runs the workspace suite; `channel-email` is in `zeroclaw-channels`' default channels, so the email tests run there. `Lint` runs clippy on the same code.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** the IMAP session in `fetch_new` is a TLS `async_imap::Session`, so the test checks the FETCH item the function sends (`new_mail_fetch_item`) rather than a server's flag state. The flag effect of `RFC822` is RFC 3501 behavior the startup drain already relies on.
- **Commands run and tail output:**

```text
$ cargo fmt --all -- --check
(clean)

$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-channels --all-targets -- -D warnings \
    -A clippy::needless_borrows_for_generic_args -A deprecated
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s)

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels --lib email
test result: ok. 87 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 1888 filtered out
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** `new_mail_fetch_marks_seen_only_in_active_mode` fails on the old behavior (`left: "BODY.PEEK[]"`, `right: "RFC822"`) and passes with the fix. The restart duplicate was first reported from a GreenMail setup where the same message id was dispatched before and after a reload. **Not verified:** against a live IMAP server on this head.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** clippy reports `needless_borrows_for_generic_args` in files this PR does not touch on my local stable 1.99 toolchain (CI pins 1.98.0), so I allowed that lint and `deprecated` locally. The pre-push hook (`cargo test --workspace`) was skipped with `--no-verify`; required CI runs the same suite.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes. The visible change is that active mode now leaves live mail marked read on the server; users who need the mailbox untouched already have `observer_mode = true`.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No

prs.title: fix(security): block high-risk shell commands even when allowlisted
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:** `validate_command_execution_for_shell` skipped the `block_high_risk_commands` gate when a command was a literal `allowed_commands` entry, so the reported profile with the hard block on and `rm` in its allowlist could execute `rm -rf` after shell auto-approval. The gate now applies to every high-risk command, which is what the config schema documents the field to do. The Balanced and Locked Down preset help and the PowerShell sandboxing guidance are reworded in the same change, because they promised an explicit-allowlist exemption the code no longer gives.
- **Scope boundary:** The allowlist itself, the medium-risk approval gate, and the supervised high-risk approval gate are unchanged. The `"*"` + `block_high_risk_commands = false` escape hatch is unchanged.
- **Blast radius:** `SecurityPolicy::validate_command_execution_for_shell`, which the shell tool, the skill shell tool, and cron shell jobs all call. A profile that allowlists a high-risk command with the hard block on now gets it blocked instead of executed.
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #11058
- **Labels:** `bug`, `config`, `domain:security`, `needs-maintainer-review`, `risk:high`, `runtime`, `security:policy`, `size:S`, `tool:delegate`.

### What this does, simply

A profile lists the commands an agent may run in `allowed_commands`. Putting a command there used to do two things at once: it allowed the command, and if the command was high-risk it also switched off the `block_high_risk_commands` hard block for that command. Only the first effect is documented, and the second is how an allowlisted `rm` ran silently while the profile had the hard block turned on.

The config schema documents `block_high_risk_commands` as "Block high-risk commands even when allowlisted", so this makes the code match that sentence. The allowlist still decides whether a command may run at all; the hard block just applies on top of it. If you do want a high-risk command to run, `block_high_risk_commands = false` is the switch for that, and it's untouched.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test

- **Reviewer testing requested?** `N/A` — this is a pure policy function covered by the crate's own unit and integration tests; a manual agent run would exercise the same function without adding signal.

### How I tested

On `master`, before the change, the existing `validate_command_explicit_rm_bypasses_high_risk_block` passed. It builds a policy with `autonomy = Full`, `allowed_commands = ["rm"]`, `block_high_risk_commands = true` and asserts `validate_command_execution("rm -rf /tmp/test", true)` returns `Ok(CommandRiskLevel::High)`. That is the silent-execution path from the issue: the command clears validation and the shell tool runs it.

I added `validate_command_blocks_explicitly_allowlisted_high_risk` (its comment quotes the schema sentence) and ran it before touching the code:

```
running 1 test
test policy::tests::validate_command_blocks_explicitly_allowlisted_high_risk ... FAILED

---- policy::tests::validate_command_blocks_explicitly_allowlisted_high_risk stdout ----
thread '...' panicked at crates/zeroclaw-config/src/policy.rs:6588:13:
expected the hard block, got: Command requires explicit approval (approved=true): high-risk operation
```

That failure is the bug. The allowlist entry cleared the hard block, so an unapproved call fell through to the approval gate instead of being blocked; with `approved = true` the call returns `Ok` and the command runs.

After the change, on the tested revision:

```
$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-config
test result: ok. 1775 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out   (lib)
     Running tests/comment_writer.rs        — 8 passed; 0 failed
     Running tests/migration.rs             — 99 passed; 0 failed
     Running tests/nodes_mdns_config.rs     — 5 passed; 0 failed
     Running tests/powershell_policy_probe.rs — 9 passed; 0 failed
     Running tests/repro_8636.rs            — 1 passed; 0 failed
     Running tests/schema_v4_external_saas.rs — 1 passed; 0 failed

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-config --lib validate_command
test result: ok. 15 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 1760 filtered out

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib independent_delegate_denies_prompt_required_skill_tools_without_approval_route
test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 5698 filtered out

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib tools::shell::tests
test result: FAILED. 64 passed; 1 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 5634 filtered out
# shell_child_cannot_open_owners_controlling_terminal is the failure: its own
# openpty() call returns EACCES in this sandbox before any ZeroClaw code runs,
# and the same denial reproduces with a standalone libc call outside the repo.
# The other 64 pass.

$ cargo fmt --all -- --check
(clean)

$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-config --all-targets -- -D warnings
(clean)

$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-runtime --all-targets -- -D warnings
(clean)

$ scripts/ci/docs_quality_gate.sh
0 error(s)

$ scripts/ci/docs_links_gate.sh
No added links detected in changed docs lines.
```

The `validate_command` set covers the three cases the issue names: a high-risk command with an explicit allow entry is blocked for both `approved` values; an ordinary allowlisted command (`ls`) still returns `Ok(Low)` without approval; a high-risk command that is not allowlisted still fails with `Command not allowed by security policy`. One test also pins the opt-out: with `block_high_risk_commands = false`, an allowlisted `rm` still returns `Ok(High)`.

Five existing tests needed to move with the policy. Three asserted the old exemption directly and now assert the block. Two PowerShell allowlist-path tests set `block_high_risk_commands = false` so they keep exercising the path-match rule they exist for rather than the high-risk gate. `independent_delegate_denies_prompt_required_skill_tools_without_approval_route` used an allowlisted `rm` to reach the approval gate, so its fixture now turns the hard block off; with it on the command would stop at the high-risk gate instead of the prompt.

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** the Rust quality gate (fmt + clippy) and the workspace test job cover the changed crate and its callers.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** None.
- **Commands run and tail output:** listed above.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** I confirmed the risk classifier and the allowlist both live in `SecurityPolicy`, so the change sits in the function that owns the decision and covers all three callers (`tools/shell.rs`, `tools/skill_tool.rs`, `cron/mod.rs`) rather than one entry point. I did not run a live agent turn against a real model.
- **Visual interface evidence:** `N/A`
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `c29e071cfd325c5b7bb6e6e14d016c54b21e8bba`, `zeroclaw-config` and `zeroclaw-runtime`, Linux x86_64, Rust 1.97.0. The branch is rebased onto current `master` (`d03325172eb6c64272f01042b60fd7f66d74c711`), so these runs are against the merged result rather than the old base.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? `No`
- New external network calls? `No`
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? `No`
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? `No`
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? `No`
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: `N/A`

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? `No`
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? `No`
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? `No`
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: exact upgrade steps for existing users: keep `block_high_risk_commands = true` to retain the hard block. Profiles that previously relied on an explicit high-risk exemption will now receive `Command blocked: high-risk command is disallowed by policy`, with no process spawned. Choosing `block_high_risk_commands = false` permits allowlisted high-risk commands subject to the remaining approval, path and sandbox checks, but is an explicit security opt-out rather than an equivalent migration. With `"*"` in the allowlist, it also admits other high-risk commands and disables the existing shell syntax restrictions. Removing the wildcard and enumerating intended commands avoids that wildcard syntax bypass, but changes the previous broad low-risk allowance. This also affects allowlisted PowerShell executables classified as high risk.

  The Windows default profile is where a stock install feels this. `runtime.shell` defaults to PowerShell on Windows (#10956), and under PowerShell a command name the classifier doesn't recognize is high risk. 18 of the 27 entries in the Windows default allowlist are high risk, including `python`, `node`, `grep`, `find` and `where`. The `default` and `locked_down` profiles set `block_high_risk_commands = true`, so on Windows those 18 move from an approval prompt to a hard block that approval can't override, and a stock Windows install can no longer run them. POSIX defaults are essentially unaffected: the same names classify as low risk under the POSIX classifier. `block_high_risk_commands = false` restores them under the ordinary approval gates.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** revert the merged change using its landed commit SHA
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** none beyond the existing `block_high_risk_commands`; reverting restores the old allowlist exemption.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** shell tool results containing `Command blocked: high-risk command is disallowed by policy` for a command the profile previously allowlisted, with no process spawned.

milestone.title: v0.9.0
milestone.description:
v0.9.0 prioritizes opt-in OIDC dashboard sign-in, principal isolation, schema V4 and a CLI-only build option.

The standard build keeps the working in-process dashboard. Sign-in stays off by default, preserving the existing pairing flow. Release gates are real-provider sign-in evidence; the five principal-isolation repairs (#11234, #11220, #11225, #11230, #11266, with #11198 tracked); schema V4 (#11218); and a build-time CLI-only option that omits gateway/web assets and directs dashboard users to the standard build.

Scoped dashboard chat has a November 3 go/no-go, with sign-in alone as the fallback. November 10 is the earliest target, subject to the gates, not a committed date.

Standalone zeroclaw-gw, full gateway IPC route/parity work, cross-process webhook handling and two-process desktop packaging move to v0.9.x. Channel listeners remain in core under existing documented exceptions. These deferrals do not complete the remaining gateway roadmap.

Source of truth: #7432 (https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/issues/7432), current release allocation. Existing implementation trackers keep their detailed work. Feature acceptance, current-head review/CI, recorded placement decisions and the v0.8.7-tag hold on breaking work remain in force.

prs.title: fix(web): correct personality editor copy for channels
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions)
- **What changed and why:** the Personality editor intro claimed personality-file edits land on the next message on every surface and never need a daemon reload. Channel agents build their base system prompt once when the daemon starts (`crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/orchestrator/mod.rs`), so a dashboard edit never reaches a channel conversation until the daemon restarts or `/admin/reload` runs. The copy now states each surface's real behavior.
- **Scope boundary:** copy only. No runtime, channel, orchestrator, or personality-loading behavior changes; #11698 keeps ownership of the per-session snapshot work on the `Agent::turn` path.
- **Blast radius:** one English i18n value in `web/src/lib/i18n.ts`. The key exists only in the `en` table; the other locale tables have no entry for it and continue to fall back to English.
- **Linked issue(s):** Fixes #12175

### What this does, simply

The Personality editor told operators that editing a markdown file such as `AGENTS.md` would reach their channel agents on the next message. It does not: channels read those files once when the daemon starts, so a channel agent keeps using the old text. The panel now says dashboard and CLI sessions pick the change up on the next message, while channel agents need a daemon restart (or `/admin/reload`) before they see it.

One follow-up note: when #11698 lands, dashboard sessions move to a per-session snapshot as well, so the dashboard sentence will need a one-line refresh at that point. This PR matches the behavior on `master` today and the wording requested in #12175.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** `N/A`; this is a single localized string whose correctness is established by reading the change and the checks below, not by an interface flow.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `web` (Personality editor intro text).
- **Setup / preconditions:** none.

### How I tested

Changed value and the consumer that renders it:

```console
$ git diff --stat
 web/src/lib/i18n.ts | 2 +-
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)

$ grep -n "personality.editor_intro" web/src/lib/i18n.ts
819:    'personality.editor_intro': "These markdown files shape your agent's voice and context. Dashboard and CLI sessions pick up changes on the next message. Channel agents read them when the daemon starts — restart the daemon (or call /admin/reload) to push an edit to channels.",

$ grep -n "editor_intro" web/src/components/sections/PersonalityEditor.tsx
339:        {t('personality.editor_intro')}
```

No stale copy or duplicate locale entry remains:

```console
$ grep -rn "no daemon reload needed" . --exclude-dir=.git
$ grep -c "personality.editor_intro" web/src/lib/i18n.ts
1
```

The edited module still parses (esbuild, TypeScript loader inferred from the file):

```console
$ esbuild web/src/lib/i18n.ts --format=esm --outfile=/dev/null
  ../../dev/null  875.8kb
⚡ Done in 42ms
```

Sourced from github/codeql-action/init's releases.

v4.39.1

  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.27.3. #4256

v4.39.0

  • Breaking change: Bump the minimum required CodeQL bundle version to 2.20.7. #4205
  • The codeql-action/analyze step now validates that a correct argument for the checkout_path input has been provided. The checkout_path input must be set to the path where the repository that is being analyzed is checked out at on the runner, if that path is something other than the workspace root. If the path does not point to a repository checkout or is different from the path that was used by codeql-action/init, then the CodeQL Action now produces a warning. #4148
  • Resolved an issue with third-party caching implementations that prevented caches from being restored correctly. #4206
  • The codeql-action/start-proxy step that is used in Code Scanning Default Setup now finds CodeQL releases using the same logic as codeql-action/init. This primarily benefits customers who are using GitHub instances other than github.com where the codeql-action/start-proxy step may previously have been unable to locate recent releases and ended up using outdated versions of the private registry authentication proxy as a result. #4198

v4.38.3

  • Upcoming breaking change: CodeQL version 2.21.2 and earlier were discontinued on 24 September 2026 alongside GitHub Enterprise Server 3.17, and will be unsupported by the next minor release of the CodeQL Action. Added a deprecation warning for customers using these versions of CodeQL. #4188
  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.27.2. #4203
  • Fixed a bug where the decision of whether to use a per-language bundle did not account for custom configurations that reference queries outside of compiled CodeQL packs. This issue was caught during internal testing and did not affect any customer repositories. We will resume the roll out of per-language bundles in the coming weeks. #4184

v4.38.2

  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.27.1. #4160

v4.38.1

  • The CodeQL Action now has experimental support for CodeQL releases for which per-language bundles are available. Per-language bundles support analysis for a single language and are therefore smaller than the combined bundles that allow analysis for all supported languages. As a result, per-language bundles take up less space on disk and are faster to download. We expect to roll this change out to everyone in the coming weeks. #4146

prs.title: docs(skills): enqueue squash merges through the merge queue
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - `master` now requires the GitHub merge queue (squash, batched). The queue tests each PR against the exact result it will land on, so it is the freshness check. The skill's freshness rules are removed, including this PR's first-version rule that required checks start after the `master` head.
  - The squash commit is now title-only: the repository's squash settings are PR title (GitHub appends ` (#N)`) and a blank body. The commit-history body, its scratch file, and the `--subject`/`--body-file` flags are removed. The PR title must be conventional before enqueuing.
  - The preflight stays: open, not draft, review decision, required CI, `do-not-merge`/`status:blocked`/`release-gate` holds, milestone and release-line placement, closing issues, and the last-moment release recheck.
  - New Step 2: refuse to enqueue when the PR title or commits carry bot or AI attribution (the same pattern the skill already used for the squash body).
  - The final step enqueues with `gh pr merge <N> --squash --auto --match-head-commit <sha>`. Verification waits for `MERGED`, or reports the `RemovedFromMergeQueueEvent` reason and stops without enqueuing it again.
  - Bypassing the queue (`--admin`) happens only on the user's explicit request for that PR, and the skill states the stale risk first. It never falls back to a bypass on its own.
  - Batches: enqueue each PR after its own preflight and confirmation; the queue serializes them.
- **What changed from the first version, and why:** The first version added a rule that every required check start after the current `master` head. That disqualified green checks after every unrelated `master` commit and did not prove which base was tested, as RFC #11096 pointed out. With the merge queue back on, the queue answers that question on the exact result, so this PR now removes the freshness rules instead of tightening them.
- **Scope boundary:** Skill text only. No workflow, ruleset, or CI changes.
- **Blast radius:** Maintainers and agents using the squash-merge skill. Merges go through the queue; commit messages on `master` are the PR title plus ` (#N)`.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #11096. Related #10815. Related #11066.
- **Labels:** `docs`, `type:docs`, `risk:medium`, `size:XS`, `needs-author-action`

### What this does, simply

The merge checklist still checks that a PR is approved, green, not on hold, and on the right release line, and now also that its title and commits carry no AI attribution. Then, instead of merging, it puts the PR in the merge queue, which tests the exact result and lands it or kicks it out, and the checklist reports which.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A — skill text; the new snippets are reproducible from the file.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** Docs gates on the changed Markdown; no code paths change.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** The local docs gates lint `docs/` and do not select `.claude/skills/squash-merge/SKILL.md`, so the changed file relies on CI's markdown checks. No PR has gone through the queue yet (the newest `merge_group` run predates it being re-enabled), so the enqueue and removal paths are checked against the API schema and live PR data, not an actual queue run.
- **Commands run and tail output:**

```text
scripts/ci/docs_quality_gate.sh      # exit 0
scripts/ci/docs_links_gate.sh        # exit 0
scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh   # exit 0
git diff --check                     # exit 0
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Ran the new snippets verbatim against the live repo. The attribution check is silent on #11084 and prints #11106's `Co-Authored-By: Claude Code <noreply@anthropic.com>` trailers. The queue status query returns `state`, `isInMergeQueue`, `mergeQueueEntry`, `autoMergeRequest` and the removal timeline for #11084. Confirmed the queue (`mergeMethod: SQUASH`) and the repository squash settings (`PR_TITLE` / `BLANK`) before writing the text. `gh pr merge --help` confirms that on a queue branch it enqueues when checks pass and enables auto-merge otherwise.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A — no user-visible interface.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** No Rust checks; no Rust changed.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

Rollback: `git revert <sha>`.

prs.title: fix(cli): refuse to run when an agent's shell spawned the process
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:** The `zeroclaw` CLI carries the operator's authority — it loads, decrypts and rewrites `config.toml`, and no agent policy exists anywhere in the process. An agent that shells out to it therefore acts with the operator's privileges, not its own, and `zeroclaw config set agents.x.risk_profile yolo` is a one-call escalation. Nothing in the risk profile prevents it: on `balanced` (the default preset) the call passes every gate — the command name matches the `["*"]` allowlist, `zeroclaw` is in neither the high- nor medium-risk table so the risk gate is inert, and a dotted config path is not `looks_like_path` so no forbidden-path argument is found. `locked_down` blocks it only incidentally, by having a real allowlist that omits the name.
- The shell tool, skill tools, and cron shell jobs now set `ZEROCLAW_AGENT_SHELL` on every command they spawn, and the CLI refuses to run when it sees it. Deliberately **not** keyed on the existing `ZEROCLAW_SESSION_ID`, which is only injected on scoped turns and would leave one-shot and webhook paths silently unmarked.
- The check binds the caller, not the command name, so copying or renaming the binary does not shake it off. It refuses **every** subcommand rather than a "safe" subset — `config get` on a secret decrypts it, so reads exfiltrate as surely as writes escalate.
- A new `presets` test pins the escalation matrix (`locked_down` refused, `balanced`/`yolo` allowed), so the justification for this guard is checkable rather than asserted.
- **Scope boundary:** Does not change the risk-profile model, the allowlist, or `balanced`'s `allowed_commands = ["*"]`. It adds one refusal at the CLI entry point plus the env marker on agent-spawned commands.
- **Blast radius:** The CLI's pre-dispatch path and the three command-spawning sites (shell tool, skill tools, cron). An operator's own terminal is unaffected (no marker present); an empty marker is treated as absent so a stray `export ZEROCLAW_AGENT_SHELL=` cannot lock the operator out.
- **Linked issue(s):** None.
- **Labels:** `bug`, `core`, `config`, `cron`, `runtime`, `tests`, `domain:security`, `tool:shell`, `risk:high`, `size:S`, `cli`, `distinguished contributor`, `needs-author-action`

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `surface: cli`
- **Setup / preconditions:** A configured install with a `balanced` agent.
- **Steps to run:** From inside an agent turn, have the agent run a shell command that invokes `zeroclaw config set …` (or set `ZEROCLAW_AGENT_SHELL=1` in the environment and run any `zeroclaw` subcommand manually to simulate the spawned context).
- **Expected on this branch (after):** The CLI refuses with a message explaining it will not run when spawned by an agent shell; nothing is read or written.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** The same `zeroclaw config set agents.x.risk_profile yolo` succeeds and escalates the agent to operator authority.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** `cargo test` (the `presets` matrix test and the CLI refusal component tests), `clippy`, `fmt`.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** None.
- **Commands run and tail output:**

```
cargo test -p zeroclaw-config -p zeroclaw-runtime
test result: ok. 1193 passed; 0 failed
test result: ok. 3483 passed; 0 failed; 2 ignored
cargo test --test component  →  214 passed
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Mutation-proven both ways: removing the CLI guard fails the two refusal tests while leaving the two negative controls (operator terminal unaffected, empty marker treated as absent) green; dropping the env marker fails the shell-tool test.
- **Limits I did NOT verify away:** an agent under a wildcard policy can `env -u ZEROCLAW_AGENT_SHELL` and get through — this raises the bar and turns a silent success into a deliberate act, it is not a proof. The deeper issue is that `balanced` sets `allowed_commands = ["*"]`, which makes *no* command-name control fully reliable; the CLI is the instance found, not the whole class.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? **No** (it removes an unintended one).
- New external network calls? **No**
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? **No**
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? **No**
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? **No**
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: This PR closes a privilege-escalation path (agent → operator authority via the CLI). Mitigation is the env-marker refusal described above; the residual `env -u` bypass is documented, not hidden.

prs.title: fix(zerocode): make Shift+Tab match its default bindings
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - Shift+Tab did nothing in zerocode on real terminals. Terminals report it as `BackTab` with Shift set (crossterm 0.29 does this for the legacy `CSI Z` sequence in `event/sys/unix/parse.rs`, for the enhanced keyboard protocol, and on Windows), while the default bindings are `BackTab` with no modifiers and `Chord::matches` compares modifiers exactly.
  - Three default bindings never fired: Config's previous sub-tab (`config_tab.section_prev`), Dashboard's previous tab (`dashboard.prev_tab`), and the quickstart modals' previous field (`quickstart_modal.prev_field`). The Config and Dashboard help overlays list Shift+Tab.
  - `strip_redundant_shift` now treats the Shift as implied by `BackTab`, the way it already does for shifted glyphs, so bindings and events compare the same way. A Shift+Tab captured in the binding editor (which records the event verbatim) also renders once as `Shift+Tab` instead of `Shift+Shift+Tab`.
  - Active key capture now receives the event before Config section navigation. The guard reads the editor's existing capture state; normal navigation resumes after capture completes.
- **Scope boundary:** `BackTab` matching/display and key-capture precedence in Config. No binding, action, or override format changes; a `shift+tab` written by hand in a keybinding override still parses as Tab with Shift, which terminals never send.
- **Blast radius:** zerocode key dispatch for `BackTab`. Ctrl+Shift+Tab and other combinations keep their own modifiers, so they still do not match a bare `BackTab` binding.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #11263 (its Config docs avoid promising Shift+Tab because of this bug).
- **Labels:** (maintainer-applied)

### What this does, simply

Shift+Tab is meant to go back one sub-tab in Config, one tab on the Dashboard, and one field in the quickstart forms, and the Config and Dashboard help say so, but pressing it did nothing. The terminal sends Shift+Tab with the Shift key marked as held, and zerocode only accepted it without that mark. This makes zerocode accept the key the way terminals actually send it.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `surface=tui`
- **Setup / preconditions:** Any running daemon of the same version.
- **Steps to run:** Open zerocode, go to the Config tab, press Shift+Tab. Repeat on the Dashboard tabs and inside a quickstart modal form. In Config's Zerocode Keybindings editor, start recording a binding and press Shift+Tab.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** Ordinary Shift+Tab moves backward in each navigation context. During key capture it records the binding without changing Config sections, and the resulting binding row displays `Shift+Tab` once.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** Shift+Tab does nothing in all three places.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** Required hosted checks are pending at the current head. Local checks cover the complete Zerocode package.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** No new manual Windows terminal run. The regression sends the terminal-shaped `BackTab + SHIFT` event through production dispatch and checks the final rendered output.
- **Commands run and tail output:** Current head `092efefe6bfcaf5649646cc7fe3230f3bcac0a54`, integrating master `1c1cd118ac536a1dd1bc79b9cce69cbdc04e4f29`:

```text
cargo fmt --all -- --check
# passed
cargo clippy --locked -p zerocode --all-targets -- -D warnings
# passed
cargo test --locked -p zerocode
# 57 library tests passed
# 1,569 binary tests passed; 2 ignored
# 3 integration tests passed
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** The original PR recorded a manual 80x24 PTY run at `5a6fbb2fda`: sending `ESC [ Z` left Config unchanged on its master baseline, while this branch moved from `zeroclaw` to `zerocode` and back. That historical observation was not repeated for this maintenance update.
- **Visual interface evidence:** Production-path rendered-output regression.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** Current head; `config_manager::tests::shift_tab_capture_precedes_config_navigation_and_renders_once` enters capture through `ConfigApp::handle_key`, verifies the saved binding, renders through `draw_into`, and checks subsequent ordinary reverse navigation.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** Final rendered binding row contains `config_tab.section_prev -> Shift+Tab`; the test rejects `Shift+Shift+Tab`. No screenshot attachment is claimed.
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** Shift+Tab stays in the Keybindings editor while capture is active and persists the binding. The next ordinary press changes Config sections. Removing only the capture guard failed the section-preservation assertion before the master integration; the unchanged regression passes on the current head.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** No full workspace rerun locally; the final change is confined to four Zerocode files. Independent review checked both merge-conflict resolutions preserve master's editor-key and paste behavior.

- New external network calls? `No`

- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? `No`
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? `No`
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: N/A

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? `Yes`

- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? `No`
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: N/A

prs.title: test(runtime): keep lib tests out of the real ~/.zeroclaw
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions)
- **What changed and why:**
  - 43 `zeroclaw-runtime` lib tests built their config from `Config::default()`, whose `data_dir` and `config_path` resolve to `ZEROCLAW_CONFIG_DIR`, else `$HOME/.zeroclaw`. On a machine with a live install, `cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib` therefore opened and wrote the operator's `data/sessions/sessions.db`, `data/sessions/acp-sessions.db` and `data/memory/brain.db`, wrote `data/state/memory_hygiene_state.json`, and created empty `agents/{agentic,alpha,caller,process-message-reassembly-agent,target}/workspace` directories (`SecurityPolicy::for_agent` creates the agent workspace under the config's install root). Three doctor tests also took `auth-profiles.lock` and read `auth-profiles.json` in the real config dir, and four `diagnose()` tests created and removed a write-probe file in the real data dir whenever that dir exists.
  - The agent turns some of these tests start can also run memory hygiene against that data dir with the default retention (archive after 7 days, prune conversation rows and purge archives after 30), not the operator's configured retention. Hygiene is on by default and runs at most every 12 hours.
  - Each affected fixture now roots `data_dir` and `config_path` in a per-test `TempDir`, reusing the module's existing isolated-config helper where there is one: `isolated_run_test_config` in `agent::loop_`, `config_with_install_root` in `doctor`, `test_config` in `tools`. The `subagent` and `tools::spawn_subagent` config helpers now return their `TempDir`, and `tools::delegate` roots the bounded approval probe, the cost-ceiling test and `config_with_narrowed_target`. Assertions are unchanged.
- **Scope boundary:** Test code only. No production code, config schema, or `Config::default()` resolution changes. I did not add a binary-wide test default: `cfg(test)` in `zeroclaw-runtime` cannot reach `Config::default()` in `zeroclaw-config`, and an env-var or feature override would also hide the default path resolution from the tests. Tests that only read the default paths without writing (for example `exists()` checks) are unchanged. Other crates were not audited; `agents/{agent-alpha,agent-beta,only-agent}` directories in a developer install match aliases used by the `zeroclaw-channels` ACP server tests, so that crate may need the same treatment.
- **Blast radius:** `zeroclaw-runtime` unit tests in `agent/loop_.rs`, `agent_lifecycle.rs`, `doctor/mod.rs`, `subagent/mod.rs`, `tools/delegate.rs`, `tools/mod.rs` and `tools/spawn_subagent.rs`. Fixture state moves from the default install to per-test temp dirs that are removed on drop.
- **Linked issue(s):** None. Related #11354, which gives fixed `$TMPDIR` fixtures in the same crate a per-test `TempDir` (disjoint files).
- **Labels:** `agent`, `doctor`, `runtime`, `tool:delegate`, `size:S`, `risk:low`.

### What this does, simply

ZeroClaw keeps its settings, conversation history and memory in a `.zeroclaw` folder in your home directory. Some runtime tests built their settings from the built-in defaults, which point at that real folder. Running the test suite on a developer machine with ZeroClaw installed therefore read and wrote the developer's actual conversation and memory databases, left stray agent folders behind, and could run the memory clean-up job on real data with default retention instead of the configured one. This PR gives each of those tests its own throwaway folder that is deleted when the test ends. The tests check exactly the same things as before; they just no longer touch the real install.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes, optional. CI runners have no live install, so CI cannot show writes into a real `~/.zeroclaw`.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** N/A. No runtime interface changes; `zeroclaw-runtime` unit tests only.
- **Setup / preconditions:** A scratch `HOME`. On macOS keep it out of `/tmp`, `/private/tmp` and `/private/var/folders` (where `mktemp -d` puts it): the three `security::seatbelt` integration tests create fixtures under `$HOME` and fail when `HOME` sits inside the sandbox profile's temp grants. Unrelated tests may fail under full-suite load (see below); the check is the directory listing.
- **Steps to run:** from the repository root:

  ```sh
  export CARGO_HOME="${CARGO_HOME:-$HOME/.cargo}" RUSTUP_HOME="${RUSTUP_HOME:-$HOME/.rustup}"
  FAKE_HOME="$(mktemp -d "$HOME/zc-fakehome.XXXXXX")"
  HOME="$FAKE_HOME" cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib
  find "$FAKE_HOME/.zeroclaw"
  ```

- **Expected on this branch (after):** `find: .../.zeroclaw: No such file or directory`.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** `.zeroclaw` exists and holds `data/memory/brain.db`, `data/sessions/sessions.db`, `data/sessions/acp-sessions.db`, `data/state/memory_hygiene_state.json` and `agents/{agentic,alpha,caller,process-message-reassembly-agent,target}/workspace`.

### How I tested

Machine: macOS arm64 with 18 cores, rustc 1.97.1, a target dir used by no other worktree, and `HOME` set to a new directory under the real home directory for every run. I compared master `83f0ff3805` with this branch `160eede179`.

Finding the tests: I ran the master lib test binary once per test (`--exact`, 12 at a time), each with a new empty `HOME`, and listed `$HOME/.zeroclaw` afterwards. 39 of the 5,465 tests created it, and together they produce exactly the full-suite listing above. An empty `HOME` hides writes that only happen when the directory already exists, so I repeated the per-test pass with `HOME` holding a pre-populated `.zeroclaw` tree (empty `config.toml`, `data/{memory,sessions,state,cron,sop,delegate_results}`, `agents/default/workspace`, every mtime backdated to 2020) on a revision with those 39 fixed. It flagged only the four `doctor::tests::diagnose_*` tests, whose `check_workspace` write probe touches `data/` when it exists.

| Check | Master `83f0ff3805` | This branch `160eede179` |
|---|---|---|
| Full suite, `HOME=<empty dir> cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib` | `.zeroclaw` created with the files above | `.zeroclaw` not created, 3 of 3 runs |
| The 43 changed tests, each alone, new empty `HOME` per test | 39 create `.zeroclaw` | none creates anything |
| The 43 changed tests, each alone, pre-populated `.zeroclaw` per test | not run | none adds, removes or modifies an entry |
| Full suite with the pre-populated `.zeroclaw` | not run | no entry added, removed or modified |

The only other entry the suite leaves in the scratch `HOME` is `Library/Caches/com.apple.python`, the macOS system Python bytecode cache, on both revisions.

Every full run on this branch failed 2 to 4 tests, none of them changed here. `configure_refuses_an_incarnation_replaced_under_the_lock` (#11330) and `peer_turn_cost_scope_through_execute_boundary_attributes_recipient_and_shares_budget` (#11350) failed in every full run on both revisions. Across all full runs of this change, including runs before the four `diagnose()` fixes, `run_still_closes_the_bracket_when_the_model_call_fails`, `model_provider_update_blocks_session_configure`, `model_provider_update_preserves_newer_session_override`, `a_live_config_write_reaches_the_daemon_pricing_refresher_without_a_reload` (#11349) and `shell_identity_probe_rejects_unsupported_and_stalled_helpers` failed intermittently. Each passed 5 of 5 runs alone, except the shell-identity probe at 4 of 5, which also fails alone on master. Master's full run additionally failed the three `security::seatbelt` tests, because that one used a `HOME` under `/private/var/folders`; with `HOME` under the real home directory they pass on both revisions.

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** `Test` and `Lint` build and run the changed tests on Linux with the CI feature set. `Parallel Runtime Test` repeats the runtime lib suite at 16 threads.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** CI runners start with an empty home and nothing fails a run that writes to `~/.zeroclaw`, so CI cannot catch a regression. The local A/B above covers it; a follow-up could run the parallel gate under a scratch `HOME` and fail if `.zeroclaw` appears.
- **Commands run and tail output:**

  ```text
  $ cargo fmt --all -- --check
  (exit 0)
  $ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib --tests -- -D warnings -A unused_imports
      Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized] target(s) in 1m 28s
  $ bash scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh <the 7 changed files>
  Comment hygiene gate passed.
  $ HOME="$FAKE_HOME" cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib
  test result: FAILED. 5454 passed; 3 failed; 8 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 32.78s
  $ test -e "$FAKE_HOME/.zeroclaw" && echo present || echo absent
  absent
  ```

  I allowed `unused_imports` because `use std::sync::mpsc` at `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/service/mod.rs:15` is unused in the macOS lib-test build on master as well (#11314 fixes it). Without the flag it is the only error, and the regular test build reports no other warning in the crate.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** That no changed assertion depends on the default paths. The `doctor` tests still see the `config`, `workspace` and `daemon` categories they assert; the temp data dir exists, so `check_workspace` now reports it present and writable instead of missing. The `tools` registry tests already passed an isolated root config, and only the registry's own config moved into the same temp dir. I did not run Linux or Windows locally.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A. Test-only change; no interface state changed.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `160eede179`, `zeroclaw-runtime` lib unit tests on macOS arm64.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** N/A; exact test output is above.
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** N/A; no runtime behavior changed.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** Workspace-wide `cargo clippy --all-targets`, workspace `cargo test`, and the parallel runtime gate, because only `zeroclaw-runtime` test code changed and CI runs all three.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? `No`. The tests now write only under per-test temp dirs instead of the real install.
- New external network calls? `No`
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? `No`
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? `No`
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? `No`
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: N/A

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? `Yes`. Test-only change.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? `No`
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? `No`. `tempfile` is already a dependency of `zeroclaw-runtime`.
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: N/A

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

Low-risk, test-only: `git revert <sha>` of the squash commit.

- **Fast rollback command/path:** `git revert <landed-squash-sha>`; nothing to migrate.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None
